screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of the core vocabulary from this unit: trend, structure, momentum, and the phases in between.

screens.question: Everything in this unit describes historical and current price behavior, not guaranteed future outcomes.
screens.explanation: That's the common thread across every concept in this unit.

screens.question: The building blocks of any trend classification are the sequence of swing [___] and lows.
screens.explanation: Swing highs and lows together form the basis of trend classification.

screens.question: What do trend, momentum, and structure all have in common as concepts?
options: They only apply to one specific asset class.
They all describe patterns in price behavior, not certainties about the future.
They all refer to one single specific candlestick shape.
screens.explanation: Each is a descriptive label for a pattern across multiple candles or swings.

screens.question: Match the concept to its one-line summary.
pairs: Overall direction based on the sequence of swings
Current speed and force of the move
Price breaking the established swing pattern
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the core vocabulary from this unit.

screens.template: Reading structure well means combining [__1__] with a healthy dose of [__2__] about certainty.
screens.explanation: Useful chart reading pairs descriptive skill with realistic expectations.

screens.question: The general path this unit followed:
items: Learn to classify overall trend direction from swings
Learn about momentum, pullbacks, and consolidation
Learn about breaks of structure as an early signal
Practice combining all of it while staying skeptical of guarantees
correct_order: Learn to classify overall trend direction from swings
Learn about momentum, pullbacks, and consolidation
Learn about breaks of structure as an early signal
Practice combining all of it while staying skeptical of guarantees
screens.explanation: Each lesson built on the one before it toward a fuller descriptive picture.

screens.question: Which best summarizes the overall theme of this unit?

options.label: Trend and structure are descriptive tools, not predictive guarantees
Trend and structure are meaningless and should be ignored
options.wrong_explanation: They're useful descriptive tools, just not guarantees.

options.label: Trend and structure always predict the future with certainty
options.wrong_explanation: This directly contradicts what every lesson covered.

screens.explanation: This balanced view has been the throughline of every lesson in this unit.

screens.question: What does this unit's work on price structure give you?
options: A dependable signal, as long as you confirm it with volume.
The ability to predict every future swing.
A clearer way to describe structure — not certainty about future swings.
screens.explanation: This unit builds reading literacy, not a predictive guarantee. That distinction matters.

screens.question: This unit's core skill is describing structure [___], not predicting it with certainty.
screens.explanation: Descriptive clarity, not predictive certainty, has been the throughline.

screens.question: Momentum, trend, and structure are all read together for a fuller picture.
screens.explanation: These concepts complement each other rather than standing alone.

lessons.title: What Is Support?
lessons.celebration: You understand support levels!

screens.title: Price's Floor
screens.text: Support is a price area where a chart has previously had trouble falling below.

screens.question: Support is best described as a price area where a chart has...
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of support.

screens.question: Support is often thought of as a price...
screens.explanation: The floor analogy is a common way to remember what support describes.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support this chart keeps bouncing from.
screens.explanation: The floor price keeps reacting off of is the support level.

screens.question: Why might a chart reader mark a support level on a chart?
options: To mark the single lowest price the chart has ever reached.
To guarantee price will bounce there again in the future.
To note a price area where price has reacted in the past, for reference.
screens.explanation: Support levels are historical reference points, not guarantees of future behavior.

screens.question: Match the term to its common description.
pairs: A price area where a chart has previously had trouble falling below
Price reacting upward after reaching a support area
Price falling clearly below a prior support area
screens.explanation: These three terms are commonly used together to describe price behavior around support.

screens.template: Support commonly forms where [__1__] has previously stepped in, near a price a chart has struggled to fall [__2__].
screens.explanation: Support marks a level where buying pressure has previously slowed or reversed declines.

screens.question: A simple way to mark support on a chart:
items: Look at recent price history for repeated lows
Mark price areas where price reacted more than once
Note that this is an estimate, not an exact line
Revisit and adjust as new price history comes in
correct_order: Look at recent price history for repeated lows
Mark price areas where price reacted more than once
Note that this is an estimate, not an exact line
Revisit and adjust as new price history comes in
screens.explanation: Support is an informal, evolving reference area, not a fixed rule.

screens.question: Which best describes what a "support level" tells you, on its own?

options.label: A guarantee price will stop there again
options.wrong_explanation: Past behavior at a level doesn't guarantee future behavior there.

options.label: A historical price area where downward moves have previously struggled
A rule set by an exchange
options.wrong_explanation: This is an informal chart-reading concept, not an official exchange rule.

screens.explanation: Support describes historical tendencies, not fixed, guaranteed rules.

screens.question: Can a support level be broken?
options: Yes — levels are historical tendencies, not permanent walls.
Only if the break comes on unusually high volume.
No — support holds price up by definition.
screens.explanation: Support levels get broken regularly. Treating any level as absolute is a common misconception.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support both troughs tested.
screens.explanation: The more times a level is touched and holds, the more notable it's considered.

screens.question: Support can eventually be broken and stop acting as a floor.
screens.explanation: No support level is permanent, breaks happen regularly.

screens.question: Tap both troughs that test the same support level.
screens.explanation: Candles 2 and 4 are the two troughs holding at about the same level, the "W" shape.

screens.question: Tap the first trough of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The 2nd candle is the first trough, testing support for the first time.

screens.question: Tap the second trough of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second trough, holding at the same support as the first.

lessons.title: What Is Resistance?
lessons.celebration: You understand resistance levels!

screens.title: Price's Ceiling
screens.text: Resistance is a price area where a chart has previously had trouble rising above.

screens.question: Resistance is best described as a price area where a chart has...
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of resistance.

screens.question: Resistance is often thought of as a price...
screens.explanation: The ceiling analogy is a common way to remember what resistance describes.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance this chart keeps rejecting from.
screens.explanation: The ceiling price keeps reacting off of is the resistance level.

screens.question: Why might a chart reader mark a resistance level on a chart?
options: To guarantee price will fall there again in the future.
To note a price area where price has reacted in the past, for reference.
To mark the single highest price the chart has ever reached.
screens.explanation: Resistance levels are historical reference points, not guarantees of future behavior.

screens.question: Match the term to its common description.
pairs: A price area where a chart has previously had trouble rising above
Price reacting downward after reaching a resistance area
Price rising clearly above a prior resistance area
screens.explanation: These three terms are commonly used together to describe price behavior around resistance.

screens.template: Resistance commonly forms where [__1__] has previously stepped in, near a price a chart has struggled to rise [__2__].
screens.explanation: Resistance marks a level where selling pressure has previously slowed or reversed rallies.

screens.question: A simple way to mark resistance on a chart:
items: Look at recent price history for repeated highs
Mark price areas where price reacted more than once
Note that this is an estimate, not an exact line
Revisit and adjust as new price history comes in
correct_order: Look at recent price history for repeated highs
Mark price areas where price reacted more than once
Note that this is an estimate, not an exact line
Revisit and adjust as new price history comes in
screens.explanation: Resistance is an informal, evolving reference area, not a fixed rule.

screens.question: Which best describes what a "resistance level" tells you, on its own?

options.label: A rule set by an exchange
options.wrong_explanation: This is an informal chart-reading concept, not an official exchange rule.

options.label: A historical price area where upward moves have previously struggled
A guarantee price will stop there again
options.wrong_explanation: Past behavior at a level doesn't guarantee future behavior there.

screens.explanation: Resistance describes historical tendencies, not fixed, guaranteed rules.

screens.question: Can a resistance level be broken?
options: No — resistance caps price by definition.
Yes — levels are historical tendencies, not permanent walls.
Only if the break comes on unusually high volume.
screens.explanation: Resistance levels get broken regularly. Treating any level as absolute is a common misconception.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance this chart keeps getting rejected at.
screens.explanation: The more times a level is touched and holds, the more notable it's considered.

screens.question: Resistance can eventually be broken and stop acting as a ceiling.
screens.explanation: No resistance level is permanent, breaks happen regularly.

lessons.title: Why Levels Form
lessons.celebration: You understand why support and resistance exist!

screens.title: Memory in the Market
screens.text: Support and resistance are commonly explained by the idea that traders "remember" prior price reactions and behave similarly near those levels again.

screens.question: Why do support and resistance levels form?
options: For no describable reason at all.
From patterns in trader behavior around prior price reactions.
screens.explanation: They're commonly explained by patterns in trader behavior around prior price reactions.

screens.question: A commonly cited reason levels "hold" is that traders may [___] how price reacted there before.
screens.explanation: Prior reactions at a level are commonly thought to influence trader behavior there again.

screens.question: What is a commonly cited explanation for why a prior high can act as resistance later?
options: The chart's software automatically caps price at that level.
Traders who missed selling near that high previously may be more inclined to sell there again.
The exchange enforces a rule preventing price from passing that point.
screens.explanation: This is a commonly cited behavioral explanation, not an enforced rule.

screens.question: Match the concept to a commonly cited explanation.
pairs: Buyers stepping in again near a level that held before
Sellers stepping in again near a level that held before
Traders responding similarly to prices that mattered before
screens.explanation: These are commonly cited behavioral explanations, not guaranteed mechanisms.

screens.template: These explanations are [__1__], not [__2__] laws of how markets must behave.
screens.explanation: These are useful, widely discussed explanations, not iron-clad rules.

screens.question: A simple way to think through why a level might matter:
items: Note that price reacted at this level before
Consider that traders may recall that reaction
Recognize this as a commonly cited theory, not a certainty
Watch how price actually behaves there this time
correct_order: Note that price reacted at this level before
Consider that traders may recall that reaction
Recognize this as a commonly cited theory, not a certainty
Watch how price actually behaves there this time
screens.explanation: This keeps the explanation grounded as a theory rather than an assumed guarantee.

screens.question: Which best reflects a responsible view of why levels form?

options.label: "This is a commonly cited theory about trader behavior, not a guaranteed law"
"This is a guaranteed law of how markets must behave"
options.wrong_explanation: No such guarantee exists; it's a commonly cited theory.

options.label: "There's no reason at all. It's pure coincidence"
options.wrong_explanation: There are commonly cited, reasonable explanations, even without certainty.

screens.explanation: The balanced view treats this as a reasonable theory, not an absolute law.

screens.question: Why do price levels tend to hold?
options: A strict rule of market structure that always applies.
Exchange rules that slow price down at round numbers.
Commonly cited theories about trader behavior — there's no strict universal rule.
screens.explanation: Treating a commonly cited theory as an absolute rule overstates what's actually known.

screens.question: The behavioral explanation for levels is a [___], not a proven law.
screens.explanation: It's commonly discussed as a reasonable theory, not an enforced law.

screens.question: Support and resistance levels are...
screens.explanation: They're informal, descriptive chart-reading concepts, not official exchange rules.

lessons.title: Multiple Touches
lessons.celebration: You understand how touches affect a level!

screens.title: The More It's Tested...
screens.text: A level is commonly seen as more notable the more times price has touched and reacted to it.

screens.question: How does a level touched once compare with one touched many times?
options: A level with more touches is commonly viewed as more notable.
A single touch is always the stronger level.
screens.explanation: A level with multiple touches and reactions is commonly viewed as more notable than one touched only once.

screens.question: A support or resistance level that has been tested multiple times is often described as more...
screens.explanation: More touches and reactions are commonly linked to a level being viewed as more notable.

screens.question: Why might multiple touches at the same level be noted by chart readers?
options: It suggests that level has repeatedly influenced price reactions.
It guarantees the level will never break.
It means the chart's data must be duplicated.
screens.explanation: Repeated reactions are commonly cited as one reason a level draws more attention, without guaranteeing anything.

screens.question: Match the touch count to a commonly cited description.
pairs: A single reaction, less established as a "notable" level
A more established, more closely watched level
Often described as a well-tested level
screens.explanation: These descriptions reflect how touch count is commonly discussed, without implying certainty.

screens.template: More touches can make a level feel more [__1__], but this still doesn't [__2__] it will hold again.
screens.explanation: Notability and guaranteed future behavior are two different things.

screens.question: A simple way to evaluate how "tested" a level is:
items: Count how many times price has approached that level
Note whether it reacted (bounced/rejected) each time
Compare that count to other nearby levels
Form a view on how notable it currently seems
correct_order: Count how many times price has approached that level
Note whether it reacted (bounced/rejected) each time
Compare that count to other nearby levels
Form a view on how notable it currently seems
screens.explanation: Counting touches is a simple, descriptive way to compare levels.

screens.question: Which best describes a level tested by price five separate times?

options.label: A level guaranteed to hold on the sixth touch
options.wrong_explanation: More touches don't guarantee the next reaction.

options.label: A more established, closely watched level, though not a guarantee
options.detail: More touches, more notability, still no certainty

options.label: A level that's now meaningless due to overuse
options.wrong_explanation: More touches are commonly viewed as adding notability, not removing it.

screens.explanation: More touches add notability in how a level is commonly discussed, without guaranteeing what happens next.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support this chart keeps bouncing from.
screens.explanation: The floor price keeps reacting off of is the support.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support this chart keeps bouncing from.
screens.explanation: Comparing touch counts is a simple, descriptive way to judge relative notability.

screens.question: A level with many touches is mathematically certain to hold on the next test.
screens.explanation: More touches add notability but never guarantee the next reaction.

lessons.title: Breakouts
lessons.celebration: You understand breakouts through levels!

screens.title: Leaving the Level Behind
screens.text: A breakout describes price clearly moving beyond a prior support or resistance level.

screens.question: What does a breakout tell you about what comes next?
options: The move is confirmed, so continuation is the expected outcome.
Nothing for certain — it describes the move that just happened, not the move to come.
The new direction will continue at least until price reaches the next major level.
screens.explanation: A breakout describes what just happened; it doesn't guarantee what happens next.

screens.question: When price clearly moves above a prior resistance level, it's often called a...
screens.explanation: "Breakout" is the standard term for clearing a prior ceiling.

screens.question: What does the term "breakdown" commonly describe?
options: Any red candle appearing on the chart.
Price clearly moving below a prior support level.
A chart that has stopped updating.
screens.explanation: "Breakdown" is the downside counterpart to "breakout."

screens.question: Match the term to its description.
pairs: Price clearly moves above a prior resistance level
Price clearly moves below a prior support level
Price returns to test a broken level from the other side
screens.explanation: These three terms are commonly used together when describing this kind of event.

screens.template: A breakout happens to the [__1__] of a level, while a breakdown happens to the [__2__].
screens.explanation: Direction is what distinguishes the two terms.

screens.question: A simple way to describe a breakout after the fact:
items: Identify the prior support or resistance level
Note that price closed clearly beyond that level
Check whether it stayed beyond that level afterward
Describe it as a breakout (or a failed one, if it didn't hold)
correct_order: Identify the prior support or resistance level
Note that price closed clearly beyond that level
Check whether it stayed beyond that level afterward
Describe it as a breakout (or a failed one, if it didn't hold)
screens.explanation: Confirming the move held is part of how chart readers describe breakouts after the fact.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance the price broke above.
screens.explanation: The ceiling the range held before the breakout is the resistance.

screens.question: Tap the breakout candle.
screens.explanation: This candle pushes above the range on strong momentum.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance the price broke above.
screens.explanation: Confirming the move held is part of how breakouts are described in hindsight.

screens.question: How does a breakdown relate to a breakout?
options: It's a breakout that failed and snapped back through the level.
It's a break of support that only counts on rising volume.
It's the downside counterpart — the same concept, opposite direction.
screens.explanation: Breakdown is simply the downside counterpart to breakout.

lessons.title: Fakeouts
lessons.celebration: You can recognize a false breakout!

screens.title: When the Breakout Fails
screens.text: A fakeout (false breakout) happens when price briefly moves past a level, then reverses back, the opposite of a confirmed break.

screens.question: A "false breakout" specifically means price...
options: Moved past a level and then reversed back, instead of continuing.
Never actually reached the level in the first place.
Continued strongly in the breakout direction.
screens.explanation: That reversal back into the prior range is what defines a false breakout.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance this chart keeps getting rejected at.
screens.explanation: "False" describes the failed follow-through.

screens.question: Why do chart readers commonly pay attention to false breakouts?
options: They guarantee a certain outcome every time they occur.
They're a commonly cited reason why waiting for confirmation matters, rather than reacting instantly.
They mean the chart's data is inaccurate.
screens.explanation: False breakouts are simply one commonly described risk of reacting to a level break too early.

screens.question: Match the outcome to its label.
pairs: Price breaks a level and keeps moving that direction
Price breaks a level then quickly reverses back
Price returns to test a broken level from the other side
screens.explanation: These are standard descriptive labels for different outcomes after a level is broken.

screens.template: A false breakout is described [__1__] the fact, once price has already [__2__] back.
screens.explanation: You can only classify a breakout as "false" once you've seen what happened next.

screens.question: A cautious way to think about a fresh breakout:
items: Note that price has just moved past a level
Recognize the move could continue or reverse
Wait to see whether the move holds over subsequent candles
Only then describe it as confirmed or false
correct_order: Note that price has just moved past a level
Recognize the move could continue or reverse
Wait to see whether the move holds over subsequent candles
Only then describe it as confirmed or false
screens.explanation: Patience before labeling a breakout is a commonly cited way to reduce being misled by an early false move.

screens.question: Which best describes a false breakout?

options.label: Price moved past a level and kept going for months
options.wrong_explanation: That would be a confirmed breakout.

options.label: Price never reaching the level at all
options.wrong_explanation: A false breakout requires crossing the level first, then reversing.

options.label: Price moved past a level but then reversed back into the range
options.detail: The definition of a false breakout

screens.explanation: The reversal back is the defining feature of a false breakout.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance this chart keeps getting rejected at.
screens.explanation: The ceiling price keeps failing to break is the resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance this chart keeps getting rejected at.
screens.explanation: You need to see the reversal happen before calling it a false breakout.

screens.question: Why do many chart readers wait for confirmation after a level breaks?
options: Because the break can be false, snapping back through the level.
Because a level isn't considered broken until the session closes.
Because volume data lags price by one candle.
screens.explanation: The risk of a false breakout is the common reason to wait for confirmation.

lessons.title: Retests
lessons.celebration: You understand retests of broken levels!

screens.title: Coming Back for a Second Look
screens.text: After a level breaks, price sometimes returns to that same level from the other side before continuing, commonly called a retest.

screens.question: A retest specifically refers to...
options: Price returning to a broken level from the other side.
Price approaching a level for the very first time.
Price gapping past a level without touching it.
screens.explanation: That's the definition, revisiting the level after it was already broken.

screens.question: Old resistance that gets broken is sometimes described as becoming new...
screens.explanation: A commonly cited idea is that a broken ceiling can act as a new floor, and vice versa.

screens.question: What is a retest, in simple terms?
options: A chart with no candles at all.
Price returning to touch a previously broken level before (potentially) continuing.
screens.explanation: A retest is specifically about revisiting a level that was already broken.

screens.question: Match the term to its description.
pairs: Price returns to touch that same level again
A commonly cited idea about broken ceilings
screens.explanation: These terms are frequently used together when describing this kind of price sequence.

screens.template: A retest happens [__1__] the original breakout, when price revisits the [__2__] level.
screens.explanation: The order matters, a retest only makes sense once a level has already broken.

screens.question: A simple way to describe a breakout-and-retest sequence:
items: Price breaks clearly past a level
Price pulls back to touch that same level again
Price either holds there and continues, or breaks back through
The sequence is described based on what actually happened
correct_order: Price breaks clearly past a level
Price pulls back to touch that same level again
Price either holds there and continues, or breaks back through
The sequence is described based on what actually happened
screens.explanation: Like breakouts, retests are described after the fact based on how price actually behaved.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance the price broke above.
screens.explanation: The ceiling the range held before the breakout is the resistance.

screens.question: Tap the breakout candle.
screens.explanation: This candle pushes above the range on strong momentum.

screens.question: A retest only makes sense once a level has already...
screens.explanation: Retesting implies revisiting a level after it was already broken.

screens.question: A retest is guaranteed to hold and never break back through.
screens.explanation: Retests can also fail, with price breaking back through the level.

lessons.title: Range Trading (Intro)
lessons.celebration: You understand the basic idea of a trading range!

screens.title: Bouncing Between the Lines
screens.text: A trading range describes a period where price bounces between a fairly consistent support and resistance level.

screens.question: A "trading range" describes price...
options: Bouncing between a fairly consistent support and resistance level.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of a trading range.

screens.question: The upper boundary of a trading range is commonly the level acting as...
screens.explanation: Resistance forms the upper boundary in a typical range description.

screens.question: What commonly happens at the edges of an established trading range?
options: Price has commonly reacted (bounced or rejected) at those edges before.
Price is guaranteed to break out immediately.
The chart data resets at each edge.
screens.explanation: The edges of a range are, by definition, levels where price has reacted previously.

screens.question: Match the range concept to its description.
pairs: The support side of the range
The resistance side of the range
Price clearly leaving the established range
screens.explanation: These terms describe the basic structure of a trading range.

screens.template: A trading range is bounded by a [__1__] level below and a [__2__] level above.
screens.explanation: Support and resistance together form the floor and ceiling of a range.

screens.question: A simple way to identify a trading range:
items: Look for repeated reactions near a similar low
Look for repeated reactions near a similar high
Confirm price has bounced between these levels more than once
Label that zone as a trading range
correct_order: Look for repeated reactions near a similar low
Look for repeated reactions near a similar high
Confirm price has bounced between these levels more than once
Label that zone as a trading range
screens.explanation: Multiple touches on both sides is what distinguishes a range from a brief pause.

screens.question: Which best describes a trading range, as commonly used?

options.label: A guarantee price will break out imminently
options.wrong_explanation: Ranges can persist for a long time before resolving.

options.label: Price bouncing between a fairly consistent support and resistance level
The exact same thing as a single candlestick pattern
options.wrong_explanation: A range spans many candles, not one shape.

screens.explanation: A trading range specifically describes bounded, repeated bouncing between two levels.

screens.question: What eventually happens to an established trading range?
options: It resolves into a breakout in one direction or another.
It resolves in the direction of the move that formed it.
It holds indefinitely, since both boundaries are proven.
screens.explanation: Treating any market phase as permanent overstates what is really a temporary description.

screens.question: A trading range is bounded by what?
options: Consistent support below and resistance above.
Support below, with no defined ceiling.
screens.explanation: Two horizontal boundaries — a floor and a ceiling — define a range.

screens.question: A trading range can persist for a long time before finally breaking out.
screens.explanation: Ranges are commonly described as lasting a while before eventually resolving.

lessons.title: Combining Levels with Trend
lessons.celebration: You can combine levels and trend context together!

screens.title: Reading Levels in Context
screens.text: Support and resistance are commonly read alongside the broader trend, not in isolation from it.

screens.question: Support and resistance levels should always be read completely independently of the overall trend.
screens.explanation: Levels are commonly read alongside trend context for a fuller picture, not in total isolation.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the highest high.
screens.explanation: Levels are commonly discussed in relation to the broader trend they sit within.

screens.question: Why might a support level be viewed differently during an uptrend versus a downtrend?
options: The broader trend context can add to how a level is commonly interpreted.
The trend has to be identified before any level can exist.
Support only exists during uptrends and never during downtrends.
screens.explanation: Combining level and trend context is commonly described as giving a fuller picture than either alone.

screens.question: Match the combined context to a commonly cited description.
pairs: Sometimes read as aligning with the broader upward structure
Sometimes read as aligning with the broader downward structure
Read with extra caution, given the conflicting context
screens.explanation: These are common (not certain) ways trend and levels are discussed together.

screens.template: Combining [__1__] and [__2__] together is commonly described as giving a fuller picture than either alone.
screens.explanation: Neither concept alone captures everything; combining them is the commonly cited habit.

screens.question: A simple way to combine levels and trend context:
items: Identify the broader trend direction first
Identify nearby support or resistance levels
Note whether the level aligns with or goes against the trend
Factor both pieces into your overall description
correct_order: Identify the broader trend direction first
Identify nearby support or resistance levels
Note whether the level aligns with or goes against the trend
Factor both pieces into your overall description
screens.explanation: This habit builds a fuller, combined read rather than relying on just one concept.

screens.question: Draw the uptrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Connecting the rising candles traces the uptrend line.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the highest high.
screens.explanation: In this uptrend the last candle prints the highest high.

screens.question: Draw the uptrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Together, levels and trend context are commonly described as more complete than either alone.

screens.question: A level that goes against the broader trend is commonly read with extra caution.
screens.explanation: Conflicting context (level vs trend) is commonly treated as worth extra caution.

lessons.title: Levels Drill, Support or Resistance?
lessons.celebration: You can classify levels across a mixed set of charts!

screens.title: Practice Round
screens.text: Practice identifying where support and resistance levels sit relative to price.

screens.question: Where is the support level in this chart, in relation to price?
options: There is no support shown in this chart
Above, where price hasn't yet traded
Below, where price has bounced more than once
screens.explanation: Support is the price floor where a chart has previously had trouble falling below.

screens.question: Where is the resistance level in this chart, in relation to price?
options: There is no resistance shown in this chart
Above, where price has struggled to close beyond

lessons.title: What Is a Double Top?

screens.title: Two Peaks at the Same Level
screens.text: A double top is commonly described as price rising to a level, pulling back, rising to about the same level again, then turning down, an "M" shape. It's read as a possible reversal after an up-move.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Two peaks at the same level forming an "M" is a double top. A head & shoulders would have three peaks with a higher middle; an ascending triangle has a flat top with rising lows.

screens.explanation: The shared high both peaks reach is the resistance level of a double top.

screens.explanation: The two peaks of a double top reach roughly the same price — that shared level is the resistance.

screens.question: Match each part of the double top to what it is.

A pullback before the second attempt

screens.explanation: These three parts together make the "M" shape.

screens.question: What does a double top describe, on its own?

options.label: That the two peaks must match to the exact cent
options.wrong_explanation: 'About the same' level is the standard, not exact equality.

options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes; it doesn't guarantee the next move.

options.label: Price tested a level twice and failed to break above it

lessons.title: The Neckline
lessons.celebration: You understand the neckline!

screens.title: The Level That Confirms
screens.text: The neckline is the level at the dip of a double top (or the peak of a double bottom). The pattern is commonly said to "complete" only if price breaks that neckline.

screens.question: In a double top, where does the neckline sit?
options: Across the tops of the two peaks.
At the midpoint of the peaks' wicks.
At the dip between the two peaks.
screens.explanation: The neckline is the low between the peaks; breaking it is what confirms the pattern.

screens.question: Why is the neckline important when reading a double top?
options: The neckline guarantees the direction of the next candle.
The neckline marks the taller of the two peaks.
The pattern is commonly said to complete only when price breaks the neckline.
screens.explanation: Breaking the neckline is the commonly cited confirmation step, descriptively.

screens.question: When is a double top commonly said to be confirmed?
options: When the second peak fails to exceed the first by any amount.
The instant the second peak prints at the same level as the first.
screens.explanation: Confirmation is tied to the neckline breaking, not just the second peak appearing.

screens.question: Match the pattern to where its neckline sits.

The commonly cited confirmation of either pattern
screens.explanation: The neckline is the shared "confirmation level" for both patterns.

screens.explanation: The two troughs at the same support form the double bottom's "W".

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance both peaks stall at.
screens.explanation: The neckline in a double bottom runs along the bounce high between the two troughs.

screens.question: How does the neckline differ between a double top and a double bottom?
options: Only the double top has one; a double bottom is confirmed by its second trough.
In a double bottom the neckline sits below the troughs rather than above them.
It's the same idea mirrored — the level whose break confirms the pattern.
screens.explanation: Both patterns share the neckline-confirmation idea, just on opposite sides.

options: The pattern is automatically confirmed anyway.
The pattern isn't commonly considered confirmed yet.
The neckline moves to a random new level.
screens.explanation: Confirmation is tied specifically to the neckline break.

screens.title: The Neckline Break
screens.text: A head & shoulders is commonly said to "confirm" only when price breaks the neckline after the right shoulder. Until then, it's a forming pattern, not a completed one.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline of this head & shoulders.

screens.question: What's the single biggest skill this unit builds?
options: Reading a three-peak (or three-trough) structure and its confirmation level together.
screens.explanation: Combining structure and confirmation is the core skill from this unit.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline.
screens.explanation: The line under the two troughs is the head & shoulders neckline.

screens.question: Tap the head.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head, the tallest of the three peaks.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two troughs that form the neckline.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 5 are the troughs on either side of the head, connected by the neckline.

lessons.title: What Is an Ascending Triangle?
lessons.celebration: You can spot an ascending triangle!

screens.title: Flat Top, Rising Lows
screens.text: An ascending triangle is commonly described as a flat resistance on top with rising lows underneath, price squeezing up toward the level. It's read as a possible continuation upward.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called an...
screens.explanation: A FLAT top with rising lows is an ascending triangle. A symmetrical triangle has both lines converging; a rising wedge rises but its lines converge rather than one staying flat.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance the highs keep testing.
screens.explanation: The flat top of an ascending triangle is the resistance being tested repeatedly.

screens.question: Tap every candle that closes at one of the rising lows.
screens.explanation: Candles 1, 2, and 4 mark the sequence of rising lows squeezing up under the flat top.

screens.question: An ascending triangle has rising lows underneath a flat resistance.
screens.explanation: Rising lows squeezing up under a flat top define the ascending triangle.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance the highs keep testing.
screens.explanation: Rising lows plus a flat top is the defining structure.

screens.question: What does an ascending triangle describe, on its own?

options.label: That the top is falling
options.wrong_explanation: The top is flat, not falling.

options.label: A guaranteed breakout up
options.wrong_explanation: Triangles can break either way; nothing is guaranteed.

options.label: Buyers pushing lows higher while sellers hold a flat level, a squeeze

screens.explanation: An ascending triangle describes a squeeze. Context, not certainty.

screens.question: Tap the three touches of the flat resistance.
screens.explanation: The flat top of an ascending triangle is the resistance being tested.

screens.question: An ascending triangle's lows are commonly described as rising.
screens.explanation: Rising lows squeezing up under a flat top is the ascending triangle shape.

screens.question: What is squeezing together in an ascending triangle?
options: Price, between a flat resistance and rising lows.
screens.explanation: Price is squeezed between the flat top and the rising lows.

screens.question: Tap the candles that touch the flat resistance on top.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push up into the flat resistance.

lessons.title: What Is a Descending Triangle?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a descending triangle!

screens.title: Flat Bottom, Falling Highs
screens.text: A descending triangle is the mirror: a flat support on the bottom with falling highs above, price squeezing down toward the level. It's read as a possible continuation downward.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: A flat support with falling highs is the descending triangle shape.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat support the lows keep testing.
screens.explanation: The flat bottom of a descending triangle is the support being tested repeatedly.

screens.question: Tap every candle that closes at one of the falling highs.
screens.explanation: Candles 1, 2, and 4 mark the sequence of falling highs squeezing down over the flat bottom.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat support the lows keep testing.
screens.explanation: Falling highs plus a flat bottom is the defining structure.

screens.question: The chart above shows a flat top with rising lows.
screens.explanation: A descending triangle has a flat BOTTOM with falling highs, the opposite.

screens.question: A chart shows a flat bottom with falling highs. What is it?
screens.explanation: Which side is flat separates the two: an ascending triangle has a flat top with rising lows.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat support the lows keep testing.
screens.explanation: The flat bottom of a descending triangle is the support being tested.

screens.question: A descending triangle's highs are commonly described as falling.
screens.explanation: Falling highs squeezing down onto a flat bottom is the descending triangle shape.

screens.question: What is squeezing together in a descending triangle?
options: Price, between falling highs and a flat support.
screens.explanation: Price is squeezed between the falling highs and the flat bottom.

lessons.title: What Is a Symmetrical Triangle?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a symmetrical triangle!

screens.title: Both Sides Converging
screens.text: A symmetrical triangle has lower highs and higher lows converging toward a point. Neither side is flat. It's read as a squeeze that can break either way.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Both sides converging (no flat side) is a symmetrical triangle.

screens.question: A symmetrical triangle has lower highs and [___] lows converging together.
screens.explanation: Lower highs and higher lows narrowing is the symmetrical shape.

screens.question: A symmetrical triangle has one perfectly flat side.
screens.explanation: Neither side is flat. Both converge. A flat side would make it ascending or descending.

screens.question: How does a symmetrical triangle differ from an ascending one?

options.label: They are identical
options.wrong_explanation: One has a flat side, the other doesn't.

options.label: Both sides converge; an ascending triangle has a flat top
options.detail: No flat side vs a flat side

options.label: A symmetrical triangle only has rising lows
options.wrong_explanation: It has lower highs too, both converging.

screens.explanation: A symmetrical triangle converges on both sides; ascending/descending have one flat side.

screens.question: A symmetrical triangle has [___] flat side(s).
screens.explanation: Both sides converge in a symmetrical triangle. Neither is flat.

screens.question: A symmetrical triangle can break either upward or downward.
screens.explanation: Without a flat side biasing one direction, a symmetrical triangle can resolve either way.

screens.question: What distinguishes a symmetrical triangle from ascending/descending ones?
options: Neither side is flat. Both converge toward a point.
It has no lower boundary at all.
screens.explanation: Lacking a flat side is what makes it "symmetrical" rather than ascending or descending.

lessons.title: The Flat Side Is the Level
lessons.celebration: You can find the level in a triangle!

screens.title: Read the Flat Side
screens.text: In ascending and descending triangles, the flat side is a support or resistance being tested again and again. Marking that level is a key reading skill.

screens.question: Tap the candles that touch the flat resistance on top.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push up into the flat resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance in this ascending triangle.
screens.explanation: The repeated highs mark the flat resistance level.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support in this descending triangle.
screens.explanation: The repeated lows mark the flat support level.

screens.question: In an ascending triangle, the flat side is a...
options: resistance level being tested by the highs.
support level being tested by the lows.
screens.explanation: The flat top of an ascending triangle is a resistance being retested.

screens.question: In a descending triangle, the flat side is a support level.
screens.explanation: The flat bottom of a descending triangle is a support being retested.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat support the lows keep testing.
screens.explanation: Repeated tests of the flat side is what makes it a meaningful level.

screens.question: Marking the flat side of a triangle is the same skill as marking any other support/resistance level.
screens.explanation: The flat side of a triangle is simply a support or resistance level, read the same way.

lessons.title: Which Way Does It Break?
lessons.celebration: You can read triangles without over-predicting!

screens.title: Bias, Not Certainty
screens.text: Ascending triangles are commonly associated with an upward break and descending with a downward break. But triangles can break either way. It's a bias, never a guarantee.

screens.question: What does an ascending triangle tell you about the eventual break?
options: It's commonly associated with an upward break, but it can break either way.
It guarantees an upward break once price reaches the flat resistance.
It guarantees a downward break, since the rising lows run out of room.
screens.explanation: It's commonly associated with an upward break, but nothing is guaranteed. It can break either way.

screens.question: What's the honest way to read an ascending triangle's direction?
options: It's commonly associated with an upward break, but can still break down.
screens.explanation: A commonly-cited bias isn't a guarantee; triangles can break either way.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance the highs keep testing.
screens.explanation: Descriptive bias, not a promise, is the honest read.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance the triangle presses against.
screens.explanation: The flat ceiling the rising lows squeeze toward is the resistance.

screens.question: Tap the three touches of the flat resistance.
screens.explanation: Even a commonly associated direction is just a bias, not a promise.

screens.question: A descending triangle can still break upward, despite the commonly cited downward bias.
screens.explanation: Bias describes a tendency, not a guarantee, any triangle can break either way.

screens.question: Tap the candles that touch the flat resistance on top.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push up into the flat resistance.

lessons.title: Triangle Identification Drill
lessons.celebration: You can classify triangles fast!

screens.text: Read each chart and name the triangle.

screens.explanation: Flat bottom with falling highs is descending.

screens.explanation: Lower highs and higher lows converging, no flat side, is symmetrical.

screens.explanation: The flat top is the resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat support the triangle presses against.
screens.explanation: The flat floor the falling highs squeeze toward is the support.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat support the lows keep testing.
screens.explanation: Repetition across mixed triangle charts builds faster recognition.

screens.question: All three triangle types share the idea of price squeezing into a narrower range.
screens.explanation: Squeezing into a narrowing range is the shared idea across ascending, descending, and symmetrical triangles.

screens.question: Tap the candles that touch the flat resistance on top.

lessons.title: Triangles Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered triangles!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of ascending, descending, and symmetrical triangles.

screens.question: Match each triangle to its shape.
pairs: Lower highs and higher lows converging
screens.explanation: The flat side (or lack of one) names each triangle.

screens.template: Ascending and descending triangles each have one [__1__] side; a symmetrical triangle has [__2__].

screens.question: What do all three triangles have in common?
options: They all guarantee an upward breakout.
They describe price squeezing into a narrowing range before a break.
They all have a flat top.
screens.explanation: A converging squeeze is the shared idea; break direction isn't guaranteed.

screens.question: Which best summarizes triangles?

options.label: A squeeze into a narrowing range, with a break-direction bias, not a guarantee
Shapes that always break upward
options.wrong_explanation: Triangles can break either way; only a flat side hints at bias.

options.label: Patterns that guarantee the breakout direction
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

screens.explanation: A squeeze with a bias (not a guarantee) is the throughline.

options: Any sideways drift between two prices.
Converging trendlines, or one flat side.

lessons.title: What Is a Bull Flag?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a bull flag!

screens.title: Pole, Then a Pause
screens.text: A bull flag is a strong up move (the pole) followed by a small, gentle pullback (the flag) that drifts down or sideways, then price often continues up. It's a continuation pattern.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: A strong pole then a small drift is a bull flag. An ascending triangle has a flat top with rising lows (no pole); a rising wedge is a converging drift, not a sharp pole plus pause.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: The 1st candle begins the strong up move, the pole.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 4 are the small downward drift after the pole, the flag itself.

screens.question: In a bull flag, the strong initial up-move is called the...
screens.explanation: The pole is the sharp initial move; the flag is the small pause after it.

screens.question: A bull flag is commonly described as a continuation pattern.
screens.explanation: The small pause after the pole often continues in the pole's direction.

screens.question: What does a bull flag describe, on its own?

options.label: A strong move, a small pause, and often continuation the same way
A guaranteed continuation
options.wrong_explanation: It's a common tendency, not a guarantee.

options.label: A reversal down
options.wrong_explanation: A bull flag is a continuation-up pattern, not a reversal.

screens.explanation: A bull flag describes a pause in an up-move that often continues. Context, not certainty.

screens.question: The strong initial move in a bull flag is called the...
screens.explanation: "Pole" is the sharp initial up-move before the small pause.

screens.question: A bull flag's pause commonly drifts down or sideways, against the pole.
screens.explanation: The flag portion drifts gently against the pole's direction before often continuing.

screens.question: What commonly happens after a clean bull flag's pause?
options: Price often continues in the pole's original (upward) direction.
screens.explanation: Continuation of the pole's direction is the commonly cited tendency after a flag.

lessons.title: What Is a Bear Flag?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a bear flag!

screens.title: The Mirror Image
screens.text: A bear flag is a strong down move (the pole) followed by a small drift up (the flag), then price often continues down. It's the bull flag's mirror.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: A strong down pole plus a small upward flag is a bear flag.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: The 1st candle begins the strong down move, the pole.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 4 are the small upward drift after the pole, the flag itself.

screens.question: A bear flag drifts slightly UP against a strong down-move.
screens.explanation: The flag drifts gently against the pole's direction, up, in a bear flag.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: Like the bull flag, it's a continuation of the pole's direction.

screens.question: A sharp move down, then a small drift upward. What is it?
screens.explanation: The pole's direction names the flag. A down pole makes it a bear flag.

screens.question: The strong initial move in a bear flag is called the...
screens.explanation: "Pole" is the sharp initial down-move before the small pause.

screens.question: A bear flag's pause commonly drifts up, against the pole.
screens.explanation: The flag portion drifts gently against the pole's direction (up, in a bear flag) before often continuing.

screens.question: What commonly happens after a clean bear flag's pause?
options: Price often continues in the pole's original (downward) direction.
screens.explanation: Continuation of the pole's direction is the commonly cited tendency after a flag.

lessons.title: Pole and Flag
lessons.celebration: You can read the parts of a flag!

screens.title: Two Parts
screens.text: Every flag has two parts: the pole (a sharp, strong move) and the flag (a small consolidation drifting against it). The flag is much smaller than the pole.

screens.question: Match each part of a flag to its description.
pairs: The small consolidation drifting against the pole
Price often resuming the pole's direction
screens.explanation: Pole then flag then continuation is the commonly described sequence.

screens.question: Compared to the pole, the flag is...
screens.explanation: The flag is a small consolidation relative to the strong pole.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: The first strong candle is the pole's start.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: The flag consolidates gently against the pole before continuing.

screens.question: In a flag pattern, how do the flag and pole compare?
options: The flag is usually larger than the pole.
The pole is the large move; the flag is a small pause.
They are always equal in size.
screens.explanation: The flag is a small pause; the pole is the large, strong move.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: The flag is a brief, small pause compared to the larger pole move.

screens.question: Both the pole and the flag are essential parts of this pattern.
screens.explanation: The pattern needs both the strong pole and the smaller pause (flag) to be complete.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 4 are the small downward drift after the pole, the flag itself.

lessons.title: Pennants
lessons.celebration: You understand pennants!

screens.title: A Tiny Triangle After a Pole
screens.text: A pennant is like a flag, but the pause forms a small symmetrical triangle (converging) instead of a rectangle. Same idea: a pole, a small pause, then often continuation.

screens.question: A pennant's pause looks like a small...
screens.explanation: A pennant's consolidation converges like a small symmetrical triangle.

screens.question: A pennant and a flag both follow a strong...
screens.explanation: Both are continuation pauses after a strong pole.

screens.question: Match each continuation pause to its shape.
pairs: A small rectangle drifting against the move
A brief pause after a strong pole
screens.explanation: Flag vs pennant differ in the pause's shape, not the overall idea.

screens.question: A pennant is...
options: A reversal pattern, unlike a flag.
A continuation pause, like a flag.
The same shape as a double top.
screens.explanation: Both flags and pennants are continuation pauses, not reversals.

screens.question: A pennant's pause forms a small [___] instead of a rectangle.
screens.explanation: A pennant's consolidation converges like a small symmetrical triangle, unlike a flag's rectangle shape.

screens.question: A pennant follows the same strong-pole-then-pause idea as a flag.
screens.explanation: Pennants and flags share the same underlying pole-then-pause structure, just different pause shapes.

lessons.title: Continuation, Not Reversal
lessons.celebration: You can read flags without over-predicting!

screens.title: A Pause, Then Often More
screens.text: Flags and pennants are continuation patterns, a pause that often (not always) resumes the prior move. They're clues, never guarantees.

screens.question: A bull flag guarantees price continues up.
screens.explanation: Continuation is a common tendency, not a guarantee, the flag can fail.

screens.question: The honest read of a bull flag is...
options: A pause that often continues up, but can still fail.
screens.explanation: Continuation is a tendency, not a certainty.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: They describe a pause that often continues, descriptively.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: The small drift after the strong pole is the flag.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: Both are read as pauses that often continue the prior move, not reverse it.

screens.question: A flag or pennant is guaranteed to continue the prior trend.
screens.explanation: Continuation is a common tendency, not a guarantee, the pattern can still fail.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 4 are the small downward drift after the pole, the flag itself.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: The 1st candle begins the strong up move, the pole.

lessons.title: What Is a Rising Wedge?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a rising wedge!

screens.title: Rising, But Narrowing
screens.text: A rising wedge has higher highs and higher lows, but the lines converge (the lows rise faster). Despite rising, it's commonly read as a possible reversal down.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Rising highs and lows that converge is a rising wedge.

screens.question: A rising wedge is commonly associated with a possible reversal downward, despite rising.
screens.explanation: Even though it rises, the converging structure is commonly read as weakening, a possible down reversal.

screens.question: A rising wedge has higher highs and higher lows, but the lines...
screens.explanation: Converging (narrowing) lines are what make it a wedge, not a channel.

screens.question: What makes a rising wedge different from a plain uptrend?

options.label: It has no highs or lows
options.wrong_explanation: It has both; they just converge.

options.label: Its lines converge (narrow) rather than staying parallel
It always goes straight up forever
options.wrong_explanation: The converging shape is the point.

screens.explanation: Convergence distinguishes a wedge from a parallel trend.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two highs that form the wedge's upper line.
screens.explanation: Converging (narrowing) lines are what define a wedge, unlike a parallel channel.

screens.question: A rising wedge is commonly read as a possible reversal downward, despite price rising.
screens.explanation: The converging structure is commonly read as weakening, even though price is rising.

screens.question: What happens to the space between the two lines in a rising wedge?
screens.explanation: Converging lines narrow the space between them as the wedge progresses.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two highs that form the wedge's upper line.
screens.explanation: Candles 1 and 5 mark the upper line, rising but converging with the line below it.

lessons.title: What Is a Falling Wedge?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a falling wedge!

screens.title: Falling, But Narrowing
screens.text: A falling wedge has lower highs and lower lows that converge (the highs fall faster). Despite falling, it's commonly read as a possible reversal up.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Falling highs and lows that converge is a falling wedge.

screens.question: A falling wedge is commonly associated with a possible reversal upward, despite falling.
screens.explanation: The converging structure is commonly read as a possible up reversal, even though it falls.

screens.question: A falling wedge has lower highs and lower lows, but the lines...
screens.explanation: Converging lines make it a wedge.

screens.question: What separates a falling wedge from a plain downtrend?
options: Nothing — a falling wedge is any downtrend.
Its trendlines converge, narrowing as price falls.
Its trendlines run parallel, forming a channel.
screens.explanation: The converging shape is what distinguishes a wedge from a plain trend.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two lows that form the wedge's lower line.
screens.explanation: Converging (narrowing) lines are what define a wedge, unlike a parallel channel.

screens.question: A falling wedge is commonly read as a possible reversal upward, despite price falling.
screens.explanation: The converging structure is commonly read as a possible up reversal, even though price is falling.

screens.question: What happens to the space between the two lines in a falling wedge?
screens.explanation: Converging lines narrow the space between them as the wedge progresses.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two lows that form the wedge's lower line.
screens.explanation: Candles 1 and 5 mark the lower line, falling but converging with the line above it.

lessons.title: What Is a Channel?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a channel!

screens.title: Parallel Lines
screens.text: A channel is a trend where the highs and lows move within parallel lines, an ascending channel (up) or descending channel (down). Unlike a wedge, the lines stay parallel, not converging.

screens.question: This shape is commonly called an...
screens.explanation: A rising trend within parallel lines is an ascending channel.

screens.question: Tap every candle that pushes up to the upper channel boundary.
screens.explanation: Parallel boundaries define a channel; converging ones define a wedge.

screens.question: The chart above shows a descending channel.
screens.explanation: A falling trend within parallel boundaries is a descending channel.

screens.question: Drag to draw the lower boundary of this ascending channel.

screens.question: Tap every candle that pushes up to the upper channel boundary.
screens.explanation: Candles 2, 4, and 6 rally up to touch the rising upper boundary; the others pull back to the lower one.

screens.question: Match each to whether its lines converge or stay parallel.
screens.explanation: Parallel vs converging is the key structural difference.

screens.question: Tap every candle that pushes up to the upper channel boundary.
screens.explanation: Parallel lines (not converging) define a channel.

screens.question: A channel can trend either upward (ascending) or downward (descending).
screens.explanation: Both ascending and descending channels are trends bounded by parallel lines.

screens.question: What is the key visual difference between a wedge and a channel?
options: A wedge's lines converge; a channel's lines stay parallel.
There is no difference at all.
A wedge only ever goes up; a channel only ever goes down.
screens.explanation: Converging vs. parallel lines is the defining structural difference.

lessons.title: Wedge vs. Channel
lessons.celebration: You can tell wedges and channels apart!

screens.title: Converging or Parallel?
screens.text: The key question: do the two trendlines converge (wedge) or stay parallel (channel)? That one read tells them apart.

screens.question: Two rising trendlines that stay parallel form a...
screens.explanation: Parallel lines make a channel; converging lines make a wedge.

screens.question: Two rising trendlines that converge (narrow) form a...
screens.explanation: Converging lines make a wedge; parallel ones make a channel.

screens.template: A wedge's lines [__1__]; a channel's lines [__2__].
screens.explanation: Convergence vs parallel is the deciding read.

screens.question: How do a rising wedge and an ascending channel differ?
options: A wedge converges; a channel stays parallel.
screens.explanation: A rising wedge converges; an ascending channel stays parallel, different structures.

lessons.title: More Confluence, Stronger Read

lessons.title: What Is a Gap?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a gap!

screens.title: A Jump With No Trading
screens.text: A gap is a jump in price where one candle opens well away from the previous candle, leaving an empty space with no trading in between. It often happens between sessions or on news.

screens.question: This is a...
screens.explanation: A jump leaving empty space between candles is a gap.

screens.question: Tap the gap candle.
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle opens above the prior candle's high, the gap candle.

screens.question: Tap the two candles the empty gap space sits between.
screens.explanation: The gap is the untraded space between candle 2's high and candle 3's open, so it sits between those two candles.

screens.question: Tap the gap-up candle.
screens.explanation: Price jumped, so no trades happened across the gap.

screens.question: Tap the candle that opened above the previous candle's high.
screens.explanation: That gap up leaves empty space between the prior high and this candle's open.

screens.question: A gap specifically occurs between...
options: One candle's close and the next candle's open.
One candle's high and its own low.
The open and close of the very same candle.
screens.explanation: That jump between close and next open is the defining feature of a gap.

screens.question: What best describes a gap?
options: A jump where price opens well away from the prior candle, leaving empty space.
A level tested twice by price.
A candle with a tiny body and long wicks.
screens.explanation: A gap is specifically about a jump in price, leaving no trading in between.

lessons.title: Gap Up vs. Gap Down
lessons.celebration: You can tell gap direction!

screens.title: Which Way Did It Jump?
screens.text: A gap up opens above the prior candle's high; a gap down opens below the prior candle's low. Direction is just which way the jump went.

screens.question: This is a...
screens.explanation: Opening below the prior low is a gap down.

screens.question: Tap the gap-down candle.
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle opens below the prior candle's low, the gap down.

screens.question: Tap the candle that opened below the previous candle's low.
screens.explanation: That gap down leaves empty space between the prior low and this candle's open.

screens.template: A gap [__1__] opens above the prior high; a gap [__2__] opens below the prior low.
screens.explanation: Up = above prior high; down = below prior low.

screens.question: Tap the gap candle.
screens.explanation: Opening above the prior high is what defines a gap up.

screens.question: A gap down specifically means the next candle opens...
options: Exactly at the prior candle's close.
screens.explanation: Opening below the prior low is what defines a gap down.

screens.question: What separates a gap up from a gap down?
options: The direction of the jump, above the prior high, or below the prior low.
screens.explanation: Direction of the jump is what separates the two gap types.

lessons.title: Why Gaps Happen
lessons.celebration: You understand why gaps form!

screens.title: News and Session Breaks
screens.text: Gaps commonly form when price can't trade continuously, overnight between sessions, or when news hits and the next available price is far from the last.

screens.question: Gaps commonly form because of...
options: a widening of the bid-ask spread intraday.
session breaks or news, when trading isn't continuous.
screens.explanation: When price can't trade continuously (overnight, news), the next price can be far away, a gap.

screens.question: Gaps commonly appear between sessions or around news.
screens.explanation: Non-continuous trading (overnight/news) is a common cause of gaps.

screens.question: Tap the gap-up candle.
screens.explanation: Discontinuous trading lets price jump, forming a gap.

screens.question: Tap the gap-up candle.
screens.explanation: This candle opens with a gap above the previous candle's range.

screens.question: Gaps commonly form when trading isn't...
screens.explanation: Discontinuous trading (overnight/news) lets price jump, forming a gap.

screens.question: News released while the market is closed is a commonly cited cause of gaps.

screens.question: Tap the two candles the empty gap space sits between.
screens.explanation: The gap is the untraded space between candle 2's high and candle 3's open, so it sits between those two candles.

lessons.title: The Gap Fill

screens.text: A "gap fill" is when price later returns to trade back through the empty gap space. It happens often but not always, a tendency, never a guarantee.

screens.explanation: Filling the gap means price comes back through the empty space.

Gaps often fill, but it's a tendency, not a guarantee.

screens.question: Tap the gap-up candle.

A gap that never gets touched again.

screens.question: Tap the two candles the empty gap space sits between.
screens.explanation: The gap is the untraded space between candle 2's high and candle 3's open, so it sits between those two candles.

Opens below the prior candle's low
Price returning through the gap's empty space
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's vocabulary.

screens.explanation: The gap is the untraded space between candle 2's high and candle 3's open, so it sits between those two candles.

lessons.title: What Is a Timeframe?
lessons.celebration: You understand timeframes!

screens.title: Each Candle's Duration
screens.text: A timeframe is how much time each candle represents, a 1-minute candle, an hourly candle, a daily candle. The same market looks different on different timeframes.

screens.question: A "timeframe" describes...
options: the price range each candle covers.
how much time each candle represents.
the total number of candles shown.
screens.explanation: Timeframe is the duration each candle covers (1m, 1h, 1d, …).

screens.question: The same market can look different on different timeframes.
screens.explanation: A move that's a blip on a daily chart can be a whole trend on a 1-minute chart.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the highest high.
screens.explanation: Each daily candle covers a full day, far more than a minute.

screens.question: Which is a "higher" timeframe?
screens.explanation: Higher timeframes cover more time per candle (daily > hourly > 1-minute).

screens.question: Draw the uptrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Timeframe defines the duration each candle covers.

screens.question: The same market can look different across different timeframes.
screens.explanation: A move that's a blip on a daily chart can look like a full trend on a 1-minute chart.

screens.question: What determines what a single candle represents?
screens.explanation: Timeframe determines the duration each candle summarizes.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the highest high.
screens.explanation: In this uptrend the last candle prints the highest high.

screens.question: Draw the uptrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Connecting the rising candles traces the uptrend line.

lessons.title: Higher vs. Lower Timeframe
lessons.celebration: You can compare timeframes!

screens.title: Zoomed Out vs. Zoomed In
screens.text: A higher timeframe (daily) is the zoomed-out big picture; a lower timeframe (1-minute) is the zoomed-in detail. Both describe the same market at different scales.

screens.question: The higher timeframe shows...
screens.explanation: Higher timeframes are the big-picture, zoomed-out view.

screens.question: The lower timeframe shows...
screens.explanation: Lower timeframes zoom in on fine detail within the bigger move.

screens.template: A higher timeframe is more [__1__]; a lower timeframe is more [__2__].
screens.explanation: Higher = zoomed out (big picture); lower = zoomed in (detail).

screens.question: Higher and lower timeframes describe the same market at different scales.
screens.explanation: They're the same price data viewed zoomed out vs zoomed in.

screens.question: A higher timeframe shows the [___] picture.
screens.explanation: Higher timeframes compress more history into each candle, the big picture.

screens.question: A lower timeframe shows more fine-grained detail over a shorter period.
screens.explanation: Lower timeframes zoom in, offering finer detail over less total time.

screens.question: What do higher and lower timeframes have in common?
options: Both describe the same market, just at different scales.
They each show a different stock entirely.
Only one of them is ever accurate.
screens.explanation: They're the same underlying price data, viewed at different zoom levels.

lessons.title: Trends Can Differ by Timeframe

screens.explanation: Trends can differ across timeframes for the same market.

options: Timeframes never affect how a trend appears.
The two timeframes are showing completely different assets.
The lower timeframe may just be showing a pullback within the larger uptrend.
screens.explanation: A higher-timeframe pullback can appear as its own trend when zoomed in.

lessons.title: Top-Down Reading
lessons.celebration: You understand top-down reading!

screens.title: Big Picture First
screens.text: "Top-down" reading means checking the higher timeframe first for the big-picture trend and key levels, then zooming into a lower one for detail. Context first, detail second.

Read the lower-timeframe move inside that context

Note the higher-timeframe key levels
Zoom into a lower timeframe for detail
Read the lower-timeframe move inside that context
screens.explanation: Context first (higher timeframe), then zoom in. That's top-down.

screens.explanation: Context from the higher timeframe frames how the lower-timeframe detail is read.
