screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head, the tallest of the three peaks.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two troughs that form the neckline.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 5 are the troughs on either side of the head, connected by the neckline.

screens.question: Tap the candles that touch the flat resistance on top.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push up into the flat resistance.

lessons.title: Candle Reading Round
lessons.celebration: You can read any candle!

screens.title: Tap the Candle
screens.text: Read each chart and tap the candle described.

screens.question: Tap the doji.
screens.explanation: The middle candle's tiny body with wicks both sides is the doji.

screens.question: Tap the hammer.
screens.explanation: The last candle, small body up top, long lower wick, is the hammer.

screens.question: Tap the shooting star.
screens.explanation: The last candle, small body down low, long upper wick, is the shooting star.

screens.question: Tap the engulfing candle.
screens.explanation: The larger down candle covering the prior up candle is the bearish engulfing.

screens.question: Tap the big-momentum candle.
screens.explanation: The big-bodied, near-wickless candle is the momentum (marubozu) candle.

screens.question: Tap the spinning top.
screens.explanation: The small body with even wicks on both sides is the spinning top.

screens.question: Tap the inverted hammer.
screens.explanation: A long upper wick with a small low body after a decline is the inverted hammer.

screens.question: Reading candles well means considering both body and wicks together.
screens.explanation: Body and wicks together tell the fuller story of a candle's period.

lessons.title: Multi-Candle Round
lessons.celebration: You can tap groups of candles!

screens.title: Tap All That Match
screens.text: Some reads need more than one candle. Tap every candle that matches.

screens.question: Tap BOTH peaks of the double top.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 4th candles are the two peaks at resistance.

screens.question: Tap BOTH troughs of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 4th candles are the two troughs at support.

screens.question: Tap BOTH shoulders of the head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 6th candles are the left and right shoulders.

screens.question: Tap the three touches of the flat resistance.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push into the flat resistance.

screens.question: Tap the three touches of the flat support in this descending triangle.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push down into the flat support.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two troughs that form this head & shoulders' neckline.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 5 are the troughs on either side of the head.

screens.question: Drag across the candles that make up this bull flag's pause.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 4 are the small downward drift after the pole.

screens.question: Multi-select questions ask you to identify more than one matching candle at once.
screens.explanation: That's the defining feature of this question type, unlike single tap-the-candle questions.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline.
screens.explanation: The line under the two troughs is the head & shoulders neckline.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance both peaks stall at.
screens.explanation: The shared high both peaks reach is the resistance level of a double top.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support both troughs tested.
screens.explanation: The more times a level is touched and holds, the more notable it's considered.

screens.question: Tap the first trough of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The 2nd candle is the first trough, testing support for the first time.

screens.question: Tap the second peak of the double top.
screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second peak, stalling at the same resistance as the first.

screens.question: Tap the second trough of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second trough, holding at the same support as the first.

screens.question: Tap the head.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head, the tallest of the three peaks.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance the highs keep testing.
screens.explanation: The flat top of an ascending triangle is the resistance being tested repeatedly.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat support the lows keep testing.
screens.explanation: The flat bottom of a descending triangle is the support being tested repeatedly.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: The 1st candle begins the strong up move, the pole.

lessons.title: Reversal or Continuation?
lessons.celebration: You can classify the setup type!

screens.title: Turn or Keep Going?
screens.text: Classify each chart as a reversal shape (a possible turn) or a continuation shape (a likely resume), descriptively.

screens.question: Is a head & shoulders commonly read as a reversal or a continuation shape?
options: Reversal (a possible turn after an up-move).
screens.explanation: Head & shoulders is commonly read as a reversal shape.

screens.question: Is a bull flag commonly read as a reversal or a continuation shape?
options: Continuation (a pause that often resumes up).
screens.explanation: Flags are continuation patterns.

screens.question: Is a double bottom commonly read as a reversal or continuation shape?
options: Reversal (a possible turn up after a down-move).
screens.explanation: A double bottom is commonly read as a reversal shape.

screens.question: Match each to its usual category.
screens.explanation: Reversal shapes suggest a turn; continuation shapes suggest a resume.

screens.question: Every reversal shape guarantees a reversal.
screens.explanation: Categories describe tendencies; nothing is guaranteed.

screens.question: Is a triangle commonly read as continuation, reversal, or either?
options: Either. It can break in either direction, though flat sides add a bias.
screens.explanation: Triangles can break either way, though ascending/descending triangles carry a directional bias.

screens.question: Wedges are commonly read as reversal shapes despite their sloped direction.
screens.explanation: A rising wedge (despite rising) and falling wedge (despite falling) are both commonly read as reversal-biased.

screens.question: Tap the left and right shoulders.
screens.explanation: The two outer peaks, lower than the head between them, are the shoulders.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline.
screens.explanation: The line under the two troughs is the head & shoulders neckline.

screens.question: Tap both troughs that test the same support level.
screens.explanation: Candles 2 and 4 are the two troughs holding at about the same level, the "W" shape.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support both troughs tested.
screens.explanation: The more times a level is touched and holds, the more notable it's considered.

screens.question: Tap the first trough of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The 2nd candle is the first trough, testing support for the first time.

screens.question: Tap the second trough of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second trough, holding at the same support as the first.

screens.question: Tap the head.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head, the tallest of the three peaks.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two troughs that form the neckline.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 5 are the troughs on either side of the head, connected by the neckline.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: The 1st candle begins the strong up move, the pole.

screens.question: Drag across the flag.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 4 are the small downward drift after the pole, the flag itself.

lessons.title: Putting It All Together
lessons.celebration: You can read a full chart!

screens.title: Everything at Once
screens.text: Combine pattern, level, and candle reads on each chart, the whole intermediate skillset.

screens.question: Tap both peaks of the double top.
screens.explanation: The two peaks at the same resistance form the double top's "M".

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance in this double top.
screens.explanation: The two peaks mark the resistance being tested.

screens.question: Tap the second peak.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the second peak at resistance.

screens.question: A pattern that lines up with a key level is stronger evidence than the pattern alone.
screens.explanation: Pattern-plus-level is confluence, stronger than either alone.

screens.question: What makes for the strongest chart read?
options: A single perfect pattern, read on its own.
Pattern, level, trend, and candles all pointing the same way.
The pattern plus volume, with level and trend set aside.
screens.explanation: The strongest reads combine several agreeing factors, not a lone signal.

screens.question: Tap BOTH shoulders of this head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 6th candles are the left and right shoulders.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline of this head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The neckline runs along the two troughs framing the head.

screens.question: Combining pattern, level, and candle reads gives a fuller picture than any one alone.
screens.explanation: This unit's core lesson is that combining reads (confluence) is stronger than a single factor.

screens.question: Tap the head.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head, the tallest of the three peaks.

screens.question: Drag to connect the two troughs that form the neckline.
screens.explanation: Candles 3 and 5 are the troughs on either side of the head, connected by the neckline.

lessons.title: Intermediate Mastery Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Intermediate level!

screens.title: You Can Read Charts
screens.text: You've learned patterns, levels, candles, structure, and confluence, and to read them all descriptively, never as guarantees. A final check.

screens.question: What ties this whole level together?
options: Reading charts descriptively, patterns, levels, and candles as clues, not guarantees.
screens.explanation: Descriptive, context-aware chart reading is the throughline of the level.

screens.question: Match each skill to what it reads.
pairs: Shapes like double tops, triangles, flags
screens.explanation: A recap of the three core reading skills.

screens.template: The strongest reads combine [__1__] agreeing factors, but are still [__2__] guarantees.
screens.explanation: Confluence is stronger but never a guarantee.

screens.question: Tap the breakout candle that clears the level.
screens.explanation: This candle clears the level before the retest that follows.

screens.question: Tap both peaks of the double top.
screens.explanation: The two peaks at the same resistance form the double top's "M".

screens.question: This level's core skill is combining pattern, level, and candle reads through...
screens.explanation: Confluence, combining multiple agreeing factors, has been the throughline of this level.

screens.question: Everything in the Intermediate level stays descriptive, never a guaranteed signal.
screens.explanation: This has been true across every unit in this level, description, not guarantees.

screens.question: What's the single biggest skill gained across this entire level?
options: Memorizing one guaranteed rule for every situation.
Reading charts by combining patterns, levels, and candles as descriptive, probability-based clues.
screens.explanation: Combining multiple descriptive reads is the core Intermediate-level skill.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance both peaks stall at.
screens.explanation: The shared high both peaks reach is the resistance level of a double top.

screens.question: Drag the line to the level that broke, then held on the retest.
screens.explanation: The old resistance becomes support on the retest.

screens.question: Tap the second peak of the double top.
screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second peak, stalling at the same resistance as the first.

lessons.title: Market Sessions Overview
lessons.celebration: You understand the basic session structure!

screens.title: Pre-Market and the Open
screens.text: Before the standard session, "pre-market" trading happens with thinner liquidity. "The open" is the first stretch of the standard session, commonly the most active part of the day.

screens.question: "Pre-market" refers to...
options: A period when markets are fully closed.
Trading before the standard session begins.
screens.explanation: Pre-market is the extended session before the standard open.

screens.question: Pre-market trading commonly has thinner liquidity than the standard session.
screens.explanation: Fewer participants are commonly active during pre-market hours.

screens.question: "The open" refers to the first stretch of the [___] session.
screens.explanation: "The open" describes the beginning of the standard trading session.

screens.question: Match the session period to its common trait.
pairs: Commonly the most active part of the day
The main trading hours most participants use
screens.explanation: Each session period commonly has a distinct liquidity and activity profile.

screens.question: Why is "the open" commonly considered especially active?

options.label: Pre-market prices are frozen and carried into the open
options.wrong_explanation: The open is a fresh burst of standard-hours activity, not carried-over pre-market prices.

options.label: Order flow is spread evenly across the whole day
options.wrong_explanation: Activity commonly clusters at the open and close, not evenly through the day.

options.label: Many participants who were waiting through pre-market act once standard hours begin

screens.explanation: Pent-up activity from pre-market commonly concentrates right at the open.

screens.question: How does pre-market liquidity commonly compare with the standard session?
options: Commonly heavier, as traders position early.
Identical; session timing doesn't affect liquidity.
screens.explanation: Liquidity commonly varies a great deal by session.

lessons.title: Midday Lull and Power Hour
lessons.celebration: You understand the midday lull and power hour!

screens.title: The Quiet Middle, the Busy End
screens.text: Midday ("lunch") is commonly a quieter stretch with reduced activity. "Power hour" is the final hour of the standard session, commonly picking activity back up.

screens.question: The midday period is commonly described as...
options: Quieter, with reduced activity compared to the open or close.
The single busiest period of the entire day.
A period when the market is fully closed.
screens.explanation: Midday is commonly a lull in activity between the open and the close.

screens.question: "Power hour" refers to...
options: The final hour of the standard session.
The first hour after the open.
screens.explanation: That's the standard meaning of the term.

screens.question: Power hour commonly sees activity [___] compared to the midday lull.
screens.explanation: Activity commonly increases again heading into the close.

screens.question: Match the session period to its common activity level.
pairs: Busy-quiet-busy across open, midday, and close
screens.explanation: Standard sessions commonly follow this busy-quiet-busy activity pattern.

screens.question: Why might power hour commonly see increased activity?

options.label: Activity is always lowest in the final hour
options.wrong_explanation: Power hour is commonly one of the busier periods, not the quietest.

options.label: Participants commonly position or adjust ahead of the session's close
The market briefly reopens during power hour
options.wrong_explanation: Power hour is part of the same standard session, not a reopening.

screens.explanation: End-of-day positioning is a commonly cited reason for power hour's added activity.

screens.question: Which part of the trading day is commonly the quietest?
screens.explanation: The open and power hour are the more commonly cited busy periods. Midday is the lull.

lessons.title: After-Hours Trading
lessons.celebration: You understand after-hours trading!

screens.title: After the Bell
screens.text: "After-hours" trading happens once the standard session ends, commonly with thinner liquidity, similar in spirit to pre-market, just on the other side of the day.

screens.question: "After-hours" trading refers to...
options: A period when no trading of any kind occurs.
Trading only during the standard session.
Trading after the standard session has ended.
screens.explanation: After-hours describes the extended session following the standard close.

screens.question: After-hours trading commonly has thinner liquidity, similar to pre-market.
screens.explanation: Both extended sessions commonly see reduced participation compared to standard hours.

screens.question: After-hours is the [___]-session counterpart to pre-market.
screens.explanation: Both are extended sessions, just on opposite sides of the standard hours.

screens.question: Match the extended session to its position relative to standard hours.
pairs: Commonly thinner liquidity than standard hours
screens.explanation: Pre-market and after-hours are the two extended sessions bookending the standard day.

screens.question: Why might a large order have a bigger price impact after-hours?

options.label: Order size never affects price impact
options.wrong_explanation: With thinner liquidity, size matters even more.

options.label: After-hours liquidity always exceeds standard-hours liquidity
options.wrong_explanation: The reverse is more commonly true.

options.label: Thinner liquidity commonly means the same order size has more relative price impact

screens.explanation: This connects the liquidity idea from earlier units to the after-hours session specifically.

screens.question: How does an after-hours fill commonly compare with a standard-hours fill?
options: It behaves identically to a standard-hours fill.
Thinner liquidity can leave a bigger gap between the expected and actual price.
It commonly fills at a better price, with less competition.
screens.explanation: As covered in the Orders & Execution unit, thinner liquidity commonly affects fill behavior.

lessons.title: Earnings Reports
lessons.celebration: You understand earnings reports!

screens.title: A Scheduled Information Event
screens.text: An earnings report is a company's scheduled release of financial results, commonly associated with sharply increased volatility around the release.

screens.question: An "earnings report" is...
options: A company's scheduled release of financial results.
screens.explanation: Earnings reports are scheduled releases of a company's financial performance.

screens.question: Earnings reports are commonly associated with increased volatility around the release.
screens.explanation: New information hitting the market at once commonly produces sharper price swings.

screens.question: Tap the gap-up candle.
screens.explanation: Being scheduled in advance is what distinguishes earnings from random breaking news.

screens.question: Match the event to its commonly cited trait.
pairs: Scheduled, often volatile around the release
A commonly cited example of a scheduling-driven gap
A commonly cited effect around the release
screens.explanation: Earnings connect directly back to the gaps and volatility concepts from earlier units.

screens.question: Tap the candle before the gap and the gap candle itself.
screens.explanation: The jump between candle 2's close and candle 3's open is the gap.

screens.question: Tap the gap-up candle.
screens.explanation: This candle opens with a gap above the previous candle's range.

lessons.title: Economic Releases
lessons.celebration: You understand economic releases!

screens.title: Broader Information Events
screens.text: Economic releases (like employment or inflation data) are scheduled reports about the broader economy, commonly associated with volatility across many assets at once, not just one company.

screens.question: Economic releases commonly affect...
options: Many assets at once, since they describe the broader economy.
Nothing at all in the markets.
screens.explanation: Broader economic data commonly moves many assets simultaneously, unlike company-specific earnings.

screens.question: Economic releases are commonly scheduled in advance, similar to earnings reports.
screens.explanation: Both are commonly known events with a set release time.

screens.question: Economic releases commonly affect [___] assets at once, unlike single-company earnings.
screens.explanation: Broad economic data is commonly linked to market-wide moves, not one company alone.

screens.question: Match the event type to its commonly cited scope.
pairs: Many assets across the broader market
Scheduled events commonly linked to volatility
screens.explanation: Scope (one company vs. the broader market) is the key difference between these two event types.

screens.question: Why might economic releases commonly cause broader market volatility?

options.label: They move only bonds, never stocks
options.wrong_explanation: Broad economic data commonly moves equities market-wide too, not just bonds.

options.label: They describe the broader economy, which can affect sentiment across many assets at once
They only ever affect a single company
options.wrong_explanation: That describes earnings, not economic releases.

screens.explanation: Broad economic data commonly shifts sentiment market-wide, unlike a single company's earnings.

screens.question: What do economic releases commonly affect?
options: Only the index that the company belongs to.
Only the specific company named in the report.
Many assets across the whole market.
screens.explanation: Economic releases are commonly cited as broader, market-wide events.

lessons.title: Why Volatility Spikes Around News
lessons.celebration: You understand why volatility spikes around news!

screens.title: New Information Hits at Once
screens.text: Volatility commonly spikes around scheduled news because a lot of new information gets absorbed by the market all at once, rather than gradually.

screens.question: Why does volatility commonly spike around scheduled news?
options: New information gets absorbed by the market all at once, rather than gradually.
News releases always calm the market down.
The bid-ask spread narrows sharply the moment news lands.
screens.explanation: A sudden burst of new information commonly produces sharper, faster price swings.

screens.question: Volatility spikes around news are commonly temporary, not a permanent state.
screens.explanation: Volatility commonly settles back down after the initial reaction to new information.

screens.question: Volatility spikes because information is absorbed all at [___], not gradually.
screens.explanation: A sudden burst of information, rather than a gradual release, is what commonly drives the spike.

screens.question: Match the concept to its commonly cited connection to news.
pairs: Common sources of sudden new information
A commonly cited effect of that sudden information
Another commonly cited effect around scheduled news
screens.explanation: These concepts connect back to ideas from Gaps and Market Mechanics earlier in the course.

screens.question: Which best explains why news-driven volatility is commonly temporary?

options.label: News-driven volatility never settles back down
options.wrong_explanation: It's commonly described as temporary, not permanent.

options.label: Once the market absorbs the new information, activity commonly settles back toward typical levels
The volatility comes from the spread, not the news
options.wrong_explanation: The spike is the market absorbing new information, not just a spread change.

screens.explanation: Volatility spikes are commonly read as a temporary reaction, not a lasting new state.

screens.question: What commonly happens to volatility after a news event?
options: It settles back down as the information is absorbed.
It settles down, then spikes again into the close.
screens.explanation: News-driven volatility is commonly temporary, not a permanent shift.

lessons.title: Trading Around News
lessons.celebration: You understand the cautious approach to trading around news!

screens.title: Extra Caution, Not a Guarantee
screens.text: Because of the added volatility and wider spreads commonly seen around news, many traders commonly apply extra caution, like reduced size or wider stops, rather than a rigid rule.

screens.question: A commonly cited approach around scheduled news is to...
options: Always dramatically increase size right before news.
Ignore risk management entirely during news.
Apply extra caution, like reduced size or wider stops.
screens.explanation: Extra caution around the added volatility is a commonly cited approach, not a guaranteed rule.

screens.question: Spreads commonly widen around major scheduled news.
screens.explanation: Increased uncertainty commonly widens the bid/ask spread around news events.

screens.question: Extra caution around news is a commonly cited [___], not a rigid universal rule.
screens.explanation: Different traders commonly apply this idea differently. It's a general approach, not one fixed rule.

screens.question: Match the news-related risk factor to its commonly cited behavior.
pairs: Commonly reduced by some traders around news
screens.explanation: These three factors are commonly discussed together when planning around news events.

screens.question: Why might someone reduce position size around scheduled news?

options.label: Because news guarantees a losing trade
options.wrong_explanation: News doesn't guarantee an outcome, it adds uncertainty.

options.label: Because added volatility and wider spreads can increase risk per trade around news
Because position size never matters around news
options.wrong_explanation: Size is exactly the risk lever some traders adjust.

screens.explanation: This connects the Risk Management unit's ideas directly to a real-world scenario.

screens.question: How do many traders adjust position size around scheduled news?
options: They increase it, since news commonly brings bigger moves.
They reduce it, since news commonly brings volatility and wider spreads.
They leave it unchanged; size follows account rules, not conditions.
screens.explanation: Added volatility and wider spreads around news are commonly met with extra caution, not extra size.

lessons.title: Why Charts Behave Differently by Session
lessons.celebration: You understand session-based differences in chart behavior!

screens.title: Same Asset, Different Rhythm
screens.text: The same chart can behave differently depending on the session, thinner, choppier moves in pre/after-hours; different rhythms across the open, midday, and power hour.

screens.question: Why might a chart look different during pre-market versus the standard open?
options: Liquidity and participation commonly differ by session, changing the chart's rhythm.
Pre-market always trends the opposite way to standard hours.
Charts are always identical no matter the session.
screens.explanation: Session-specific liquidity differences are commonly cited as changing how a chart behaves.

screens.question: The open, midday, and power hour commonly have different typical rhythms within the same day.
screens.explanation: Each session period commonly carries its own typical activity level, as covered earlier in this unit.

screens.question: Session context is one more form of [___] to combine with everything else you've read.
screens.explanation: Like other context factors in this course, session timing adds to (not replaces) the full read.

screens.question: Match the session to a commonly cited chart trait.
pairs: Often the most active, sometimes sharpest moves
screens.explanation: A recap of the session-based rhythm differences covered across this unit.

screens.question: Why combine session awareness with everything else you've learned?

options.label: Because it's one more piece of context that can change how a chart's move should be read
Because sessions only matter to long-term investors
options.wrong_explanation: Session rhythm is especially relevant to intraday reading.

options.label: Because session timing replaces the need for any other analysis
options.wrong_explanation: It's one added factor, not a replacement for everything else.

screens.explanation: Session context is one more descriptive factor to combine with the rest of your reading skills.

screens.question: A choppy move in pre-market looks identical to one at the standard open. Read them the same way?
options: No — pre-market moves are always reversed at the open.
Yes — identical price action carries identical meaning.
No — session context such as liquidity and participation changes the read.
screens.explanation: The same shape can carry different meaning depending on which session it happened in.

lessons.title: Trading Sessions & News Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Trading Sessions & News unit!

screens.title: Bringing It All Together
screens.text: A final review of market sessions, earnings, economic releases, news-driven volatility, and reading session context.

screens.question: Every session and news concept in this unit adds context, rather than guaranteeing an outcome.
screens.explanation: That's the common thread across every lesson in this unit.

screens.question: After-hours is the extended-session counterpart to...
screens.explanation: Reviewing the pairing from earlier in this unit.

screens.question: What do earnings reports and economic releases have in common?
options: Both are scheduled information events commonly linked to increased volatility.
Both guarantee the market moves in the reported direction.
Both affect only the single company that reports them.
screens.explanation: Both are scheduled events commonly tied to volatility, differing mainly in scope.

screens.question: Match the term to its one-line meaning.
pairs: Extended sessions with commonly thinner liquidity
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's core vocabulary.

screens.template: News commonly brings [__1__] volatility and [__2__] spreads, calling for extra caution.
screens.explanation: Higher volatility and wider spreads are the commonly cited reasons for added caution around news.

screens.question: Tap the gap-up candle.
screens.explanation: This candle opens with a gap above the previous candle's range.

screens.question: How does this unit frame news events?
options: As added volatility and context — risk to manage, not a guaranteed opportunity.
screens.explanation: This unit consistently frames news as added context and risk, never a guaranteed opportunity.

screens.question: Tap the two candles the empty gap space sits between.
screens.explanation: The gap is the untraded space between candle 2's high and candle 3's open, so it sits between those two candles.

lessons.title: What Is Risk Per Trade?
lessons.celebration: You understand risk per trade!

screens.title: How Much Is on the Line
screens.text: Risk per trade describes how much of your capital could be lost on a single trade if it goes against you.

screens.question: "Risk per trade" specifically describes...
options: How much capital could be lost on a single trade if it goes against you.
The commission charged on a single trade.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of risk per trade.

screens.question: Draw the downtrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: A bigger portion of capital at stake means a larger risk for that trade.

screens.question: Why is thinking about risk per trade useful, in general terms?
options: It helps quantify how much a single loss could realistically cost.
It guarantees the trade will be profitable.
It tells you the best price to take profit at.
screens.explanation: Quantifying potential loss is the whole point of thinking about risk per trade.

screens.question: Match the risk framing to its description.
pairs: How much could be lost on one specific trade
The combined risk across all open positions
How much loss someone is generally comfortable with
screens.explanation: These related concepts together build a fuller risk picture.

screens.template: Risking 10% of an account on one trade is generally considered a [__1__] risk than risking [__2__]%.
screens.explanation: A larger percentage risked per trade means a bigger potential impact from one loss.

screens.question: A simple way to think through risk before placing a trade:
items: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Compare that amount to your total account size
Express it as a percentage of your account
Use that percentage to inform your position size
correct_order: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Compare that amount to your total account size
Express it as a percentage of your account
Use that percentage to inform your position size
screens.explanation: This process turns an abstract risk tolerance into a concrete plan.

screens.question: Draw the downtrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Connecting the falling candles traces the downtrend line.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the lowest low.
screens.explanation: In this downtrend the last candle prints the lowest low.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the lowest low.
screens.explanation: Small, consistent risk per trade is a commonly recommended habit.

screens.question: Compared with risking a small percent, risking a large percent on one trade is...
screens.explanation: A larger percentage at risk is generally considered higher, not lower, risk.

lessons.title: Position Sizing Basics
lessons.celebration: You understand position sizing!

screens.title: How Much to Put In
screens.text: Position sizing is the process of deciding how much capital to allocate to a single trade, commonly derived from your risk tolerance.

screens.question: Position size is commonly derived from your risk tolerance and stop-loss level.
screens.explanation: A sound position size is commonly calculated backward from how much you're willing to risk.

screens.question: The amount of capital allocated to a single trade is commonly called its...
screens.explanation: "Position size" describes how much of your capital a single trade uses.

screens.question: What is a commonly cited way to calculate an appropriate position size?
options: Start from your maximum acceptable dollar risk, then work out the size that keeps a stop-loss hit within that amount.
Randomly pick a size that feels right in the moment.
Always use the same position size regardless of the stop-loss distance.
screens.explanation: Working backward from acceptable risk is a commonly cited, methodical approach.

screens.question: Match the risk concept to its description.
pairs: How much capital is allocated to a single trade
How far price can move before the risk limit is hit
The most you're willing to lose on that trade
screens.explanation: These three concepts together determine an appropriate position size.

screens.template: A wider stop-loss distance generally calls for a [__1__] position size, to keep the same dollar [__2__].
screens.explanation: If the stop is further away, a smaller size keeps the total dollar risk the same.

screens.question: A simple way to calculate position size before a trade:
items: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Decide where your stop-loss level would be
Calculate the position size that keeps the loss within that maximum if the stop is hit
Only then consider the position size final
correct_order: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Decide where your stop-loss level would be
Calculate the position size that keeps the loss within that maximum if the stop is hit
Only then consider the position size final
screens.explanation: Position size is commonly derived from your risk tolerance and stop level, not chosen randomly.

screens.question: Which of these two hypothetical trades has the better risk-to-reward ratio, as described?

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $100 (1:1)
options.wrong_explanation: Reward here is equal to risk, not more favorable.

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $300 (1:3)
options.detail: Reward is three times the risk

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $50 (2:1 against)
options.wrong_explanation: This risks more than it could potentially gain.

screens.explanation: A higher reward relative to the risk taken is generally considered a more favorable ratio, on paper.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support this chart keeps bouncing from.
screens.explanation: The floor price keeps reacting off of is the support.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support this chart keeps bouncing from.
screens.explanation: Position size is worked backward from your dollar risk and stop distance.

screens.question: To keep the same dollar risk, a wider stop calls for...
screens.explanation: A wider stop calls for a SMALLER position size to keep the same dollar risk, not larger.

lessons.title: Risk/Reward Ratio
lessons.celebration: You understand risk/reward ratios!

screens.title: What You Could Lose vs. Gain
screens.text: A risk/reward ratio compares the potential loss on a trade to its potential gain, pure math, not a signal.

screens.question: A "2:1 risk-to-reward ratio" means the potential reward is twice the potential risk.
screens.explanation: That's the standard meaning of a 2:1 (or similarly stated) risk/reward ratio.

screens.question: A trade risking $100 to potentially make $200 has a risk/reward ratio of...
screens.explanation: $100 of risk against $200 of potential reward is a 1:2 ratio (risk:reward).

screens.question: Risking $120 at a 1:3 risk/reward ratio. Drag to the potential reward.
screens.explanation: A 1:3 ratio means reward is three times the risk: 3 × $120 = $360.

screens.question: What does a favorable risk/reward ratio generally describe?
options: A guarantee that the trade will be profitable.
Potential reward that is larger than the potential risk taken.
The exact number of shares being traded.
screens.explanation: Risk/reward describes the relationship between potential loss and gain, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.question: Match the risk/reward description to its general reading.
pairs: Generally considered a more favorable ratio
Generally considered a less favorable ratio
screens.explanation: Comparing potential reward to potential risk is the core of this concept.

screens.template: A [__1__] risk/reward ratio means more potential reward for the same [__2__] taken.
screens.explanation: A higher ratio means a larger potential payoff relative to the risk.

screens.question: A simple way to calculate a trade's risk/reward ratio before entering:
items: Identify your planned entry price
Identify your planned stop-loss level (the risk)
Identify your planned target level (the reward)
Compare the two distances as a ratio
correct_order: Identify your planned entry price
Identify your planned stop-loss level (the risk)
Identify your planned target level (the reward)
Compare the two distances as a ratio
screens.explanation: This calculation can be done in advance, before a trade is even placed.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance the price broke above.
screens.explanation: The ceiling the range held before the breakout is the resistance.

screens.question: Tap the breakout candle.
screens.explanation: This candle pushes above the range on strong momentum.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance the price broke above.
screens.explanation: A higher ratio means a bigger potential payoff relative to the risk.

screens.question: A 1:3 risk/reward ratio means the potential reward is three times the potential risk.
screens.explanation: 1:3 (risk:reward) means the reward is three times the risk.

lessons.title: Stop-Loss Placement Logic
lessons.celebration: You understand where stop-losses are commonly placed!

screens.title: Not Just a Random Number
screens.text: Stop-loss placement is commonly tied to a specific reason, like a nearby support/resistance level, rather than an arbitrary number.

screens.question: A stop-loss level is commonly chosen...
options: Completely at random, with no reasoning.
Tied to a specific reason, like a nearby level.
screens.explanation: Stop-loss levels are commonly tied to a specific reason, like a nearby support or resistance level.

screens.question: Placing a stop-loss just beyond a nearby support or resistance level is a commonly cited...
screens.explanation: This is a commonly cited approach, among several, for placing a stop-loss with a clear reason behind it.

screens.question: Why might a stop-loss be placed just beyond a nearby support level?
options: It sets the stop a fixed dollar amount below entry, ignoring the level.
It guarantees the stop will never be triggered.
If that level breaks, it may suggest the original reason for the trade no longer holds.
screens.explanation: Tying the stop to a meaningful level gives it a clear, describable reason.

screens.question: Match the stop-loss placement idea to its reasoning.
pairs: Tied to a level that would invalidate the original idea
Tied to a consistent risk amount regardless of chart structure
Commonly cited as being triggered by normal price noise
screens.explanation: These are different commonly discussed approaches to stop-loss placement.

screens.template: A stop-loss placed too [__1__] may get triggered by normal price [__2__], not a meaningful shift.
screens.explanation: A stop set with too little room can be triggered by ordinary fluctuations rather than a real change in the picture.

screens.question: A simple way to think through stop-loss placement:
items: Identify the specific reason for the trade
Identify what price level would suggest that reason no longer holds
Place the stop-loss just beyond that level
Confirm the resulting risk fits your position sizing plan
correct_order: Identify the specific reason for the trade
Identify what price level would suggest that reason no longer holds
Place the stop-loss just beyond that level
Confirm the resulting risk fits your position sizing plan
screens.explanation: This ties the stop-loss to a specific reason rather than an arbitrary number.

screens.question: Which best describes a stop-loss placed "just beyond a nearby support level"?

options.label: A fixed number of cents below entry, ignoring the level
options.wrong_explanation: The point is tying the stop TO the level, not a fixed offset.

options.label: A guarantee the position will never lose money
options.wrong_explanation: A stop-loss limits risk; it doesn't guarantee no loss ever occurs.

options.label: Tied to a level that would suggest the original trade idea no longer holds

screens.explanation: Tying the stop to a meaningful level gives it a clear, describable rationale.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support this chart keeps bouncing from.
screens.explanation: The floor price keeps reacting off of is the support.

screens.question: Stop-loss placement is commonly tied to a specific [___], not a random number.
screens.explanation: A reasoned placement (like just beyond a level) is commonly recommended over an arbitrary stop.

screens.question: A stop-loss placed too close to entry can get triggered by normal price noise.
screens.explanation: A too-tight stop risks getting hit by ordinary fluctuations, not a meaningful shift.

lessons.title: Overleveraging Danger
lessons.celebration: You understand the danger of overleveraging!

screens.title: Amplifying Both Directions
screens.text: Leverage amplifies both potential gains and potential losses, overleveraging describes using more than a comfortable, risk-appropriate amount.

screens.question: What does leverage actually amplify?
options: Both potential gains and potential losses.
screens.explanation: Leverage amplifies both directions, potential gains and potential losses alike.

screens.question: Using more leverage than is appropriate for your risk tolerance is commonly called...
screens.explanation: "Overleveraging" describes taking on leverage beyond what fits your risk tolerance.

screens.question: Why is overleveraging commonly cited as a significant danger?
options: It guarantees larger profits with no added risk.
It amplifies losses, potentially causing much larger damage from a single adverse move.
It reduces risk by spreading it across more trades.
screens.explanation: Amplified losses are the commonly cited core danger of overleveraging.

screens.question: Match the leverage concept to its description.
pairs: A tool that amplifies both potential gains and losses
Using more leverage than fits one's risk tolerance
Sized to fit an individual's risk tolerance and plan
screens.explanation: Leverage itself is a neutral tool; overleveraging describes misusing it relative to one's own risk tolerance.

screens.template: Leverage can [__1__] both potential gains and potential [__2__] from the same price move.
screens.explanation: This dual amplification is the core mechanism behind leverage's risk.

screens.question: A simple way to think through leverage before using it:
items: Understand that leverage amplifies both gains and losses
Consider your own risk tolerance and capital
Choose a leverage level that fits that risk tolerance
Avoid leverage levels that would cause outsized damage from a single move
correct_order: Understand that leverage amplifies both gains and losses
Consider your own risk tolerance and capital
Choose a leverage level that fits that risk tolerance
Avoid leverage levels that would cause outsized damage from a single move
screens.explanation: This keeps leverage decisions tied to individual risk tolerance rather than chasing amplified gains alone.

screens.question: Draw the downtrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Connecting the falling candles traces the downtrend line.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the lowest low.
screens.explanation: In this downtrend the last candle prints the lowest low.

screens.question: Leverage amplifies both potential gains and potential...
screens.explanation: Leverage cuts both ways, bigger potential gains AND bigger potential losses.

screens.question: "Overleveraging" means using...
options: Leverage that fits your risk tolerance well.
More leverage than fits your risk tolerance.
screens.explanation: Overleveraging specifically means using MORE leverage than fits your risk tolerance.

lessons.title: Drawdowns
lessons.celebration: You understand drawdowns!

screens.title: The Dip From a Peak
screens.text: A drawdown measures how far an account has fallen from a prior peak value, a normal part of any trading account's history.

screens.question: A drawdown measures how far an account has fallen from its prior peak value.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of a drawdown.

screens.question: The percentage decline from an account's highest value to a subsequent low point is called a...
screens.explanation: "Drawdown" is the standard term for this kind of decline.

screens.question: Why is understanding drawdowns commonly considered useful?
options: It tells you exactly when the next losing streak will end.
It guarantees an account will never decline again.
It helps set realistic expectations that account value doesn't move in a straight line.
screens.explanation: Understanding drawdowns helps build realistic expectations about a normal account's ups and downs.

screens.question: Match the drawdown concept to its description.
pairs: The highest point an account has reached so far
A subsequent lower point after the peak
The percentage decline from peak to trough
screens.explanation: These three concepts together define how a drawdown is measured.

screens.template: Even accounts that are [__1__] over the long run commonly experience some [__2__] along the way.
screens.explanation: Drawdowns are a normal part of most account histories, even ones that end up profitable overall.

screens.question: A simple way to calculate a drawdown:
items: Identify the account's peak value so far
Identify the lowest value reached after that peak
Calculate the percentage decline between the two
Describe that percentage as the drawdown
correct_order: Identify the account's peak value so far
Identify the lowest value reached after that peak
Calculate the percentage decline between the two
Describe that percentage as the drawdown
screens.explanation: This is a straightforward, descriptive calculation based on account history.

screens.question: Draw the downtrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Connecting the falling candles traces the downtrend line.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the lowest low.
screens.explanation: In this downtrend the last candle prints the lowest low.

screens.question: A drawdown measures decline from a prior...
screens.explanation: Drawdown specifically measures decline from the account's prior peak value.

screens.question: Even profitable trading accounts commonly experience some drawdowns along the way.
screens.explanation: Drawdowns are a normal part of most account histories, even profitable ones.

lessons.title: Losing Streaks Are Normal
lessons.celebration: You understand that losing streaks happen!

screens.title: Even With a Sound Plan
screens.text: A string of losing trades in a row can happen even to a reasonable, well-thought-out approach. It's a normal part of trading, not proof of failure.

screens.question: Does a losing streak automatically prove an approach is flawed?
options: Yes, it proves the approach is broken.
No, streaks can happen even with a sound approach.
Only after ten losses in a row.
screens.explanation: Losing streaks can happen even with a reasonable approach. They don't automatically prove it's flawed.

screens.question: A string of consecutive losing trades is commonly called a losing...
screens.explanation: "Losing streak" is the standard term for this kind of consecutive-loss sequence.

screens.question: Why might a losing streak happen even with a reasonable approach?
options: No approach wins every single time; some losses in a row can occur by chance alone.
A losing streak is mathematically impossible with any sound approach.
Losing streaks only happen to beginners.
screens.explanation: Even a reasonable approach with a positive long-run track record can still see a run of losses.

screens.question: Match the concept to a commonly cited description.
pairs: A run of consecutive losing trades
The idea that some losses in a row can occur even with a sound plan
Abandoning a reasonable plan solely because of a losing streak
screens.explanation: These concepts together explain why a losing streak doesn't automatically mean a plan has failed.

screens.template: A losing streak is commonly described as [__1__], not automatic proof that a plan is [__2__].
screens.explanation: Some run of losses is statistically possible even with a reasonable, well-thought-out approach.

screens.question: A calmer way to respond to a losing streak:
items: Pause before making any big changes
Review whether the original plan was actually followed
Consider whether anything specific needs adjusting
Avoid abandoning a reasonable plan based on short-term results alone
correct_order: Pause before making any big changes
Review whether the original plan was actually followed
Consider whether anything specific needs adjusting
Avoid abandoning a reasonable plan based on short-term results alone
screens.explanation: A measured review is commonly recommended over an immediate, emotional overhaul.

screens.question: Draw the downtrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Connecting the falling candles traces the downtrend line.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the lowest low.
screens.explanation: In this downtrend the last candle prints the lowest low.

screens.question: A losing streak can happen even with a [___] approach, purely by chance.
screens.explanation: Even a sound approach can see a losing streak by chance alone.

screens.question: Does a losing streak automatically prove an approach is broken?
options: Yes, it proves the approach is broken.
No, streaks can happen by chance even with a sound approach.
Only if it lasts a month.
screens.explanation: Streaks can happen by chance; they don't automatically prove the approach has failed.

lessons.title: Capital Preservation Mindset
lessons.celebration: You understand capital preservation!

screens.title: Protecting What You Have
screens.text: Capital preservation describes prioritizing protection of existing capital, commonly viewed as foundational to being able to trade over the long term.

screens.question: "Capital preservation" describes prioritizing...
options: Maximum position size on every trade.
Avoiding all risk entirely, under every circumstance.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive meaning of a capital preservation mindset.

screens.question: Protecting your existing capital is commonly viewed as foundational to trading over the [___] term.
screens.explanation: Without capital, there's nothing left to trade with, preservation supports staying in the game long-term.

screens.question: Why might capital preservation be commonly emphasized alongside potential gains?
options: Preserving capital guarantees higher returns than any other approach.
Without sufficient capital remaining, there's nothing left to trade with going forward.
Capital preservation means avoiding trades entirely.
screens.explanation: Capital preservation is commonly linked to risk management, since capital is needed to keep participating at all.

screens.question: Match the mindset to its general focus.
pairs: Prioritizing potential gains, often with less protection
Weighing both protection and potential upside together
screens.explanation: These represent different general postures toward risk and capital.

screens.template: A capital preservation mindset is commonly linked to sound [__1__] management, not the complete avoidance of all [__2__].
screens.explanation: Preservation doesn't mean avoiding all risk. It means managing it deliberately.

screens.question: A simple way to build a capital preservation mindset into a plan:
items: Define an acceptable risk per trade in advance
Use position sizing consistent with that risk
Avoid outsized risk on any single trade
Review the overall plan periodically
correct_order: Define an acceptable risk per trade in advance
Use position sizing consistent with that risk
Avoid outsized risk on any single trade
Review the overall plan periodically
screens.explanation: These steps together support protecting capital while still participating in the market.

screens.question: Which best describes a capital preservation mindset?

options.label: Avoiding all risk entirely, under every circumstance
options.wrong_explanation: Preservation is about managing risk deliberately, not eliminating it entirely.

options.label: Prioritizing protection of existing capital as foundational to trading long-term
Guaranteeing profits no matter what
options.wrong_explanation: Preservation focuses on protecting capital, not guaranteeing gains.

screens.explanation: Capital preservation is about deliberate protection, not the total avoidance of risk or a guarantee of profit.

screens.question: Why is capital preservation commonly treated as foundational?
options: Without capital left, there's nothing to generate future gains with.
Because preserving capital raises the win rate of each trade.
Because brokers require a minimum balance to keep trading.
screens.explanation: Preservation and growth are commonly linked: staying in the game is what lets you keep pursuing gains.

screens.question: Capital preservation means prioritizing [___] of existing capital.
screens.explanation: Capital preservation is about protecting what you already have.

screens.question: Capital preservation means...
options: Avoiding all risk entirely, under every circumstance.
Managing risk deliberately, not eliminating it.
screens.explanation: It means managing risk deliberately, not eliminating it entirely.

screens.title: A Percent of the Account
screens.text: Risk per trade is commonly expressed as a percent of the account you're willing to lose on one trade, often a small figure like 1%. Keeping it small and consistent is a common risk approach.

options: a fixed number of shares every time.
a percent of the day's price range.
screens.explanation: Risk per trade is commonly set as a small percent of the account.

screens.question: Keeping risk per trade [___] and consistent is a common approach.
screens.explanation: Small, consistent risk per trade is commonly recommended.

screens.question: Risking a huge percent of the account on one trade is commonly considered high risk.
screens.explanation: A large percent at risk on one trade exposes the account to big damage from one loss.

screens.question: Why keep risk per trade small and consistent?

options.label: So position size can be as large as you like
options.wrong_explanation: Small consistent risk is the whole point; it caps size.

options.label: So a single loss can't do outsized damage to the account
So every trade is guaranteed to win
options.wrong_explanation: Sizing doesn't change win odds.

screens.explanation: Small consistent risk limits the damage any one loss can do.

screens.question: Risk per trade is commonly expressed as a [___] of the account.
screens.explanation: Risk per trade is commonly set as a small, consistent percent of the account.

screens.question: Keeping risk per trade small and consistent is a commonly recommended habit.
screens.explanation: Small, consistent risk per trade limits damage from any single loss.

So a single loss can't do outsized damage to the account.
screens.explanation: Small risk per trade limits the impact of any one loss, without guaranteeing outcomes.

screens.text: To turn a risk percent into dollars: multiply the account size by the percent. On a $10,000 account, 1% risk = $100.

On a $5,000 account, risking 2% means risking...
To get dollar risk, multiply account size by the risk...

screens.explanation: Multiplying account size by the risk percent gives the dollar risk amount.

screens.question: A larger account risking the same percent risks more dollars in absolute terms.
screens.explanation: The same percent of a bigger account is a larger dollar amount.

lessons.title: What Is 1R?

screens.title: R = The Amount Risked
screens.text: "R" is shorthand for the amount you risked on a trade. If you risk $100, then 1R = $100. Measuring results in R lets you compare trades of different sizes.

screens.question: If you risk $100 on a trade, then 1R equals...
screens.explanation: 1R is simply the amount risked, here, $100.

screens.question: "R" stands for the amount you [___] on the trade.
screens.explanation: R is the risk amount; results are measured in multiples of it.

screens.question: If you risk $250 on a trade, then 1R equals...
screens.explanation: 1R = the amount risked = $250.

screens.question: Measuring results in R lets you compare trades of different dollar sizes.
screens.explanation: R normalizes results, so a "2R win" means the same regardless of position size.

screens.question: "R" is shorthand for the amount [___] on a trade.
screens.explanation: R specifically represents the risk amount, used to measure results.

screens.question: Measuring results in R lets you compare trades of different sizes fairly.
screens.explanation: R normalizes results across different position sizes.

lessons.title: Reward in R
lessons.celebration: You can measure reward in R!

screens.title: Wins as Multiples of Risk
screens.text: A win is measured in R too. If you risk $100 (1R) and gain $200, that's a +2R result. A loss of the full risk is −1R.

screens.question: You risk $100 and the trade gains $200. That result is...
screens.explanation: A $200 gain on $100 risk is twice the risk, +2R.

screens.question: You risk $100 and the trade loses the full risk. That result is...
screens.explanation: Losing the full amount risked is −1R.

screens.question: A gain of three times your risk is a [___] result.
screens.explanation: Three times the risk gained is +3R.

screens.question: You risk $200 and gain $600. That result is...
screens.explanation: $600 gain on $200 risk is three times the risk, +3R.

screens.question: Drag the slider to the dollar gain on a +4R result, risking $150.
screens.explanation: +4R means four times the risk: 4 × $150 = $600.

screens.question: Losing exactly the amount you risked on a trade is expressed as...
screens.explanation: Losing the whole risked amount is by definition −1R.

screens.question: A gain of twice the amount risked is a [___] result.
screens.explanation: Twice the risk gained is +2R, by definition.

screens.question: A full loss of the entire risked amount is described as -1R.
screens.explanation: Losing exactly what was risked is, by definition, -1R.

screens.text: Position size is commonly worked backward from your dollar risk and stop distance: choose a size so that if the stop is hit, the loss equals your planned dollar risk.

Find the stop distance (entry price minus stop price)
Divide the dollar risk by the stop distance to get share size

screens.question: Why adjust position size to the stop distance?
options: So the dollar risk stays consistent from trade to trade.
So the share count stays consistent from trade to trade.
So the reward-to-risk ratio always stays above 2:1.
screens.explanation: A fixed size regardless of stop distance makes the dollar risk vary unpredictably between trades.

screens.question: Drag the slider to the correct position size: $200 dollar risk, $2.00 stop distance.
screens.explanation: Dollar risk ÷ stop distance = $200 ÷ $2.00 = 100 shares.

screens.question: Position size is worked [___] from your dollar risk and stop distance.
screens.explanation: You start from the risk and stop, then solve for the position size.

screens.question: To keep the same dollar risk, a wider stop distance calls for...
screens.explanation: A wider stop calls for a SMALLER size to keep the dollar risk the same, not larger.

Bigger size always means bigger profit

screens.explanation: Consistent percent risk, stop-based sizing, and R measurement is the throughline.

lessons.title: Win Rate Isn't Everything
lessons.celebration: You understand why win rate alone misleads!

screens.title: How Often vs. How Much
screens.text: Win rate is how often you win. But it ignores how much you win or lose. A high win rate with tiny wins and huge losses can still lose money overall.

screens.question: Win rate measures...
options: how much each winning trade makes.
screens.explanation: Win rate is the frequency of wins, not their size.

screens.question: A high win rate always means a profitable system.
screens.explanation: If wins are tiny and losses are huge, even a high win rate can lose overall.

screens.question: Win rate ignores how [___] you win or lose per trade.
screens.explanation: Win rate is frequency only; it ignores the size of wins and losses.

screens.question: Why isn't win rate enough on its own?

options.label: Because it ignores the size of the wins and losses
Because it's always wrong
options.wrong_explanation: Win rate is useful, just incomplete.

options.label: Because winning never matters
options.wrong_explanation: Both how often and how much matter.

screens.explanation: You need both how often (win rate) and how much (R) to judge results.

screens.question: Win rate measures how [___] you win, not how much.
screens.explanation: Win rate is purely a frequency measure, not a measure of size.

lessons.title: Combining Win Rate and R
lessons.celebration: You can combine win rate and R!

screens.title: Frequency Meets Size
screens.text: The honest picture combines win rate (how often) with average R (how much). A lower win rate can still come out ahead if the average win in R is large enough.

screens.question: To judge a system honestly, combine win rate with...
screens.explanation: Win rate plus average R (size) gives the honest picture.

screens.question: A 40% win rate can still be profitable if the average winner is large in R.
screens.explanation: Big average wins (in R) can outweigh more frequent small losses.

screens.template: Combine how [__1__] you win with how [__2__] you win to judge a system.
screens.explanation: Frequency (win rate) and size (R) together tell the story.

screens.question: A system wins 40% of the time but averages +3R on wins and −1R on losses. This can be...
options: guaranteed to lose because win rate is under 50%.
profitable overall, thanks to the large average win.
screens.explanation: Large average wins can more than offset frequent small losses.

screens.question: Combining win rate with average [___] gives the honest picture.
screens.explanation: Frequency (win rate) plus size (average R) together tell the full story.

screens.question: A 40% win rate can still be profitable if the average win in R is large enough.
screens.explanation: Large average wins can outweigh more frequent, smaller losses.

lessons.title: What Is Expectancy?
lessons.celebration: You understand expectancy!

screens.title: Average Result Per Trade
screens.text: Expectancy is the average result per trade, measured in R, over many trades. A positive expectancy means the average trade gains R over the long run.

screens.question: The commonly used steps to calculate expectancy:
items: Multiply win rate by the average win size (in R)
Multiply loss rate by the average loss size (in R)
Subtract the second result from the first
correct_order: Multiply win rate by the average win size (in R)
Multiply loss rate by the average loss size (in R)
Subtract the second result from the first
screens.explanation: (Win rate × average win) minus (loss rate × average loss) is the standard expectancy formula.

screens.question: Match each term to what it measures.
pairs: How much winning trades gain, in R
How much losing trades give back, in R
screens.explanation: These three inputs combine into the expectancy formula.

screens.question: Drag the slider to the expectancy: 40% win rate, average win +2R, average loss -1R.
Expectancy is the...
options: the percentage of trades that win.
average result per trade (in R) over many trades.
screens.explanation: Expectancy is the long-run average result per trade.

screens.question: A positive expectancy means the average trade, over many trades, gains R.
screens.explanation: Positive expectancy = the average trade comes out ahead in R over the long run.

screens.question: Expectancy is the average result per trade measured in...
screens.explanation: Expressed in R, expectancy compares across position sizes.

screens.question: Why is expectancy a long-run idea?

options.label: Because it ignores wins and losses
options.wrong_explanation: It's built from wins and losses.

options.label: Because it predicts the next trade exactly
options.wrong_explanation: It says nothing certain about one trade.

options.label: Because it's an average that only holds over many trades, not any single one

screens.explanation: Expectancy is an average over many trades, not a promise about any single one.

screens.question: Expectancy is the average [___] per trade, in R, over many trades.
screens.explanation: Expectancy is a long-run average, measured in R.

lessons.title: Winning With Under 50% Wins
lessons.celebration: You understand how low win rates can still win!

screens.title: Big Wins, Small Losses
screens.text: A system can be profitable with a win rate below 50% if its winners are much larger (in R) than its losers. Size can outweigh frequency.

screens.question: A system with a 35% win rate can still be profitable if...
options: its winners are much larger in R than its losers.
screens.explanation: Large winners in R can outweigh more frequent, smaller losers.

screens.question: Must you win more than half your trades to be profitable?
options: No, large enough winners in R can offset a sub-50% win rate.
screens.explanation: With large enough winners in R, a sub-50% win rate can still profit.

screens.question: A low win rate can still win if the [___] are much larger in R.
screens.explanation: Larger winners in R can more than offset frequent small losses.

screens.question: A system wins fewer than half its trades. Is it unprofitable?
options: Yes; a system has to win more than half its trades.
Not necessarily — large winners in R can still give positive expectancy.
Not necessarily — but only if the win rate stays above 40%.
screens.explanation: Expectancy combines win rate with average R. There's no fixed win-rate threshold that decides it.

screens.question: A system can be profitable with a win rate below [___]%.
screens.explanation: Sub-50% win rates can still be profitable if the average winner in R is large enough.

lessons.title: Sample Size Matters
lessons.celebration: You understand sample size!

screens.title: A Few Trades Prove Little
screens.text: Expectancy and win rate only mean something over a large enough sample. A handful of trades can look great or terrible purely by chance.

screens.question: Expectancy is meaningful only over...
options: a large enough sample of trades.
screens.explanation: Averages need many trades to be meaningful; small samples are noisy.

screens.question: Do three wins in a row prove positive expectancy?
options: No, a tiny sample can happen by chance.
Only with real money at stake.
screens.explanation: A tiny sample can happen by chance; it doesn't prove long-run expectancy.

screens.question: A small [___] of trades can look great or terrible purely by chance.
screens.explanation: Small samples are dominated by luck, not the true average.

screens.question: Why be careful with a small sample?

options.label: Because small samples are always accurate
options.wrong_explanation: They're the least reliable.

options.label: Because sample size never matters
options.wrong_explanation: It's central to trusting an average.

options.label: Because chance can make a few trades misleading in either direction

screens.explanation: Small samples are dominated by luck, so they can badly mislead.

screens.question: Expectancy is meaningful only over a [___] sample of trades.
screens.explanation: A large sample is needed for averages like expectancy to be meaningful.

lessons.title: Expectancy & Edge Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered expectancy & edge!

lessons.title: Trending, Ranging, or Volatile?
lessons.celebration: You can classify market conditions!

screens.title: Three Broad Conditions
screens.text: Markets are commonly classified into broad conditions: trending (directional), ranging (sideways between levels), and volatile (large, erratic swings). Reading the condition guides how you read everything else.

screens.explanation: Directional progress (higher highs/lows) is a trending-up condition.

screens.question: This condition is...
screens.explanation: Sideways between support and resistance is a ranging condition.

screens.question: This condition is...
screens.explanation: Big, erratic swings with no clear direction is a volatile condition.

screens.question: Match each condition to its description.
screens.explanation: These three broad conditions describe most markets.

screens.explanation: Trending, ranging, and volatile are the three broad commonly cited conditions.

screens.question: Reading the market condition first frames how you read everything else.

lessons.title: What Is a Moving Average?
lessons.celebration: You understand moving averages!

screens.title: The Average of Recent Prices
screens.text: A moving average (MA) is the average of the last N prices, recalculated each candle. A 20-period MA averages the last 20 closes. It's a smoothed line that follows price.

screens.question: A moving average is the...
options: average of the last N prices, updated each candle.
screens.explanation: An MA averages the most recent N prices and updates as new ones arrive.

screens.question: A 20-period moving average averages the last [___] prices.
screens.explanation: The number is how many recent prices it averages.

screens.question: A moving average updates as each new candle arrives.
screens.explanation: It's "moving" because it recalculates with each new price.

screens.question: What does a moving average give you?

options.label: The exact future value
A guarantee of the next price
A smoothed line summarizing recent price

screens.explanation: An MA smooths recent price into a line; it doesn't predict the future.

screens.question: A moving average is the average of the last [___] prices, updated each candle.
screens.explanation: An MA averages a set number (N) of recent prices, recalculating with each new one.

screens.question: A moving average predicts future prices with certainty.
screens.explanation: An MA summarizes recent price into a smoothed line. It doesn't guarantee the future.

lessons.title: Smoothing Out Noise
lessons.celebration: You understand smoothing!

screens.title: Less Jitter, Clearer Direction
screens.text: Because it averages, a moving average smooths out the candle-to-candle jitter, making the broader direction easier to see.

screens.question: Averaging recent prices makes a moving average...
options: identical to the raw price line.
screens.explanation: Averaging smooths the noise, so the line is steadier than raw price.

screens.question: A moving average [___] out short-term noise.
screens.explanation: Averaging reduces the jitter, smoothing the line.

screens.question: A longer moving average is generally smoother than a shorter one.
screens.explanation: Averaging more prices smooths more, so longer MAs are steadier.

screens.question: Smoothing makes the broader [___] easier to see.
screens.explanation: With less noise, the general direction is clearer.

screens.question: Averaging recent prices makes a moving average [___] than raw candles.
screens.explanation: Averaging reduces candle-to-candle jitter, producing a smoother line.

screens.question: Price holding above a rising MA is commonly described as relative...

screens.question: Price vs the MA is a guaranteed signal to act on.

lessons.title: Short vs. Long MAs
lessons.celebration: You understand fast vs slow MAs!

screens.title: Fast and Slow
screens.text: A short MA (few periods) reacts quickly to price. It's "fast." A long MA (many periods) reacts slowly. It's "smooth and slow." Each shows a different scale of trend.

options: fast. It reacts quickly to price.
the same as a long-period MA.
screens.explanation: Fewer periods means quicker reaction, a "fast" MA.

screens.question: A long-period MA is...
screens.explanation: More periods means slower reaction, a "slow," smooth MA.

screens.question: A short-period MA is [___]. It reacts quickly to price.
screens.explanation: Fewer periods means quicker reaction, making it a "fast" MA.

screens.question: Which moving average hugs price more closely?
screens.explanation: A SHORT MA hugs price more closely; a long MA is smoother and slower.

screens.question: Tap the candle where the fast MA crosses above the slow MA.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is where the fast (blue) MA crosses above the slow (amber) MA, a bullish crossover.

lessons.title: MA Crossovers
lessons.celebration: You understand MA crossovers!

screens.title: When Fast Crosses Slow
screens.text: A "crossover" is when a fast MA crosses a slow MA. It's commonly used as a descriptive trend cue. But MAs are lagging (built from past prices), so crossovers are not guaranteed signals.

screens.question: Tap the candle where the fast MA crosses above the slow MA.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is where the fast (blue) MA crosses above the slow (amber) MA, a bullish crossover.

screens.question: An MA crossover is when...
options: a fast MA crosses a slow MA.
screens.explanation: A crossover is the fast and slow MAs crossing each other.

screens.question: Moving averages are lagging, since they're built from past prices.
screens.explanation: An MA is an average of past prices, so it lags current price.

screens.question: Because MAs are built from past prices, they are...
screens.explanation: Averaging past prices makes MAs lag, not lead.

screens.question: Tap the candle where the fast MA crosses below the slow MA.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is where the fast (blue) MA crosses below the slow (amber) MA, a bearish crossover.

screens.question: Tap the candle where the fast MA crosses up through the slow MA.
screens.explanation: At this candle the fast average pulls above the slow one.

screens.question: Moving averages are [___] because they're built from past prices.
screens.explanation: Averaging past prices makes MAs lag current price, rather than lead it.

screens.question: An MA crossover is a guaranteed trading signal.
screens.explanation: A crossover is a descriptive, lagging cue, not a guarantee.

lessons.celebration: You've mastered moving averages!
