lessons.title: Classifying Trending Markets
lessons.celebration: You can classify a trending market!

screens.title: Recognizing a Sustained Direction
screens.text: A trending market is commonly described as one showing a sustained move in one general direction over time.

screens.question: A trending market is commonly described as showing a sustained move in one general direction.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of a trending market.

screens.question: Which chart description commonly matches a "trending" classification?
options: Price bouncing repeatedly between the same two levels with no progress either way.
A series of higher highs and higher lows (or lower highs and lower lows) over time.
A single candle with almost no wick on either side.
screens.explanation: A sustained sequence of higher (or lower) highs and lows is the commonly cited hallmark of a trend.

screens.question: A market showing a sustained move in one general direction is commonly classified as...
screens.explanation: "Trending" is the standard classification term for this kind of sustained directional move.

screens.question: Match the market condition to its commonly described classification.
pairs: Sustained higher highs and higher lows
Price oscillating with no clear progress
Sudden, erratic price swings with no clear pattern
screens.explanation: These are commonly cited classifications for describing different general market conditions.

screens.question: A commonly described general process for classifying a market as trending:
items: Look at the sequence of highs and lows over recent history
Check whether they're consistently moving in one direction
Confirm the direction has held for a meaningful stretch of time
Classify the condition as trending if those checks hold
correct_order: Look at the sequence of highs and lows over recent history
Check whether they're consistently moving in one direction
Confirm the direction has held for a meaningful stretch of time
Classify the condition as trending if those checks hold
screens.explanation: This process reflects a commonly described, descriptive way to classify market conditions.

screens.question: Draw the uptrend line from the first candle to the last.
screens.explanation: Connecting the rising candles traces the uptrend line.

screens.question: Tap the candle that makes the highest high.
screens.explanation: In this uptrend the last candle prints the highest high.

screens.question: A trending market is classified by a sustained move in one general...
screens.explanation: Sustained directional progress defines a trending classification.

screens.question: Is a single candle enough to classify a market as trending?
options: No, it needs a sustained sequence of highs and lows.
Only if it is a large marubozu.
screens.explanation: Classification needs a sustained sequence of highs and lows, not one candle.

lessons.title: Classifying Choppy Markets
lessons.celebration: You can classify a choppy market!

screens.title: Back and Forth With No Progress
screens.text: A choppy market is commonly described as one moving back and forth with no clear sustained direction.

screens.question: A "choppy" market is commonly described as...
options: Moving back and forth with no clear sustained direction.
Showing a sustained move in one general direction.
Showing unusually large, fast swings in one direction.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of a choppy market.

screens.question: Which chart description commonly matches a "choppy" classification?
options: Price oscillating within a range with no clear sustained progress in either direction.
A single sharp, one-directional move with no pullbacks at all.
A long, uninterrupted sequence of higher highs and higher lows.
screens.explanation: Oscillation with no sustained progress is the commonly cited hallmark of a choppy market.

screens.question: A market moving back and forth with no clear sustained direction is commonly classified as...
screens.explanation: "Choppy" is the standard classification term for this kind of directionless movement.

screens.question: Match the market condition to its commonly described classification.
pairs: Sustained higher highs and higher lows
screens.explanation: These are commonly cited classifications used to describe different general market conditions.

screens.question: A commonly described general process for classifying a market as choppy:
items: Look at the sequence of highs and lows over recent history
Check whether they lack a clear, sustained direction
Notice repeated back-and-forth movement without net progress
Classify the condition as choppy if those checks hold
correct_order: Look at the sequence of highs and lows over recent history
Check whether they lack a clear, sustained direction
Notice repeated back-and-forth movement without net progress
Classify the condition as choppy if those checks hold
screens.explanation: This process reflects a commonly described, descriptive way to classify market conditions.

screens.question: Which best describes a "choppy" market classification?

options.label: A guarantee that price will never move again
options.wrong_explanation: Choppy describes a pattern of movement, not an absence of movement.

options.label: Moving back and forth with no clear sustained direction
options.detail: A descriptive classification of directionless price behavior

options.label: A sustained move consistently in one direction
options.wrong_explanation: That description matches a trending classification instead.

screens.explanation: Choppy specifically describes directionless oscillation, distinct from a sustained trend or complete stillness.

screens.question: A market prints a long, clear sequence of higher highs and higher lows. How is it classified?
screens.explanation: A sustained sequence of higher highs and higher lows is commonly described as trending, not choppy.

screens.question: A choppy market moves back and forth with no clear sustained...
screens.explanation: Directionless oscillation defines a choppy classification.

screens.question: A choppy market shows...
options: No sustained direction, just back-and-forth movement.
screens.explanation: Choppy specifically describes the ABSENCE of sustained directional progress.

lessons.title: Classifying Volatile Markets
lessons.celebration: You can classify a volatile market!

screens.title: Larger, Faster Swings
screens.text: A volatile market is commonly described as one showing unusually large or fast price swings, in either direction.

screens.question: A volatile market is commonly described as showing unusually large or fast price swings.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of a volatile market.

screens.question: Which chart description commonly matches a "volatile" classification?
options: A slow, steady drift with very small price changes over a long period.
Unusually large or fast price swings, without necessarily implying a sustained direction.
A single flat candle with almost no range at all.
screens.explanation: Large or fast swings, regardless of direction, are the commonly cited hallmark of volatility.

screens.question: A market showing unusually large or fast price swings is commonly classified as...
screens.explanation: "Volatile" is the standard classification term for this kind of large or fast movement.

screens.question: Match the market condition to its commonly described classification.
screens.explanation: These are commonly cited classifications used to describe different general market conditions.

screens.question: A commonly described general process for classifying a market as volatile:
items: Look at the size and speed of recent price swings
Compare them to what's typical for that market
Notice if swings are unusually large or fast relative to that norm
Classify the condition as volatile if those checks hold
correct_order: Look at the size and speed of recent price swings
Compare them to what's typical for that market
Notice if swings are unusually large or fast relative to that norm
Classify the condition as volatile if those checks hold
screens.explanation: This process reflects a commonly described, descriptive way to classify market conditions.

screens.question: Tap the breakout candle.

screens.question: A volatile market shows unusually large or fast...
screens.explanation: Large or fast price swings define a volatile classification.

screens.question: Volatile describes swing size and speed, not necessarily direction.
screens.explanation: A volatile market can swing sharply in either direction, direction isn't the point.

lessons.title: Recognizing a Fakeout
lessons.celebration: You understand fakeout patterns!

screens.title: A Move That Doesn't Hold
screens.text: A fakeout is commonly described as a price move beyond a level that quickly reverses, rather than continuing.

screens.question: A "fakeout" is commonly described as...
options: A price move beyond a level that quickly reverses.
A price move beyond a level that keeps continuing.
Price approaching a level for the first time.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of a fakeout.

screens.question: Which chart description commonly matches a "fakeout" classification?
options: Price stays well within a range the entire time, never approaching any level.
Price briefly clears a level, then quickly reverses back rather than continuing.
Price clears a level and continues steadily in that direction afterward.
screens.explanation: A brief move beyond a level followed by a quick reversal is the commonly cited hallmark of a fakeout.

screens.question: A price move beyond a level that quickly reverses, rather than continuing, is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: "Fakeout" is the standard term for this reversal-after-clearing pattern.

screens.question: Match the pattern to its commonly described classification.
pairs: Clears a level and reverses quickly
Never approaches the level at all
screens.explanation: These are commonly cited classifications used to describe price behavior around a level.

screens.question: A commonly described general process for recognizing a fakeout after it happens:
items: Note that price cleared a previously established level
Watch what happens shortly after that clearing
Notice if price quickly reverses back rather than continuing
Classify the completed pattern as a fakeout if that reversal occurred
correct_order: Note that price cleared a previously established level
Watch what happens shortly after that clearing
Notice if price quickly reverses back rather than continuing
Classify the completed pattern as a fakeout if that reversal occurred
screens.explanation: This process reflects a commonly described, after-the-fact way to classify this pattern.

screens.question: Which best describes a "fakeout," as commonly defined?

options.label: A guarantee that every breakout will eventually reverse
options.wrong_explanation: A fakeout describes a specific completed pattern, not a rule about every breakout.

options.label: A price move beyond a level that quickly reverses, rather than continuing
A price move beyond a level that continues steadily afterward
options.detail: This describes a breakout, not a fakeout
options.wrong_explanation: That description matches the commonly described idea of a breakout instead.

screens.explanation: A fakeout specifically describes a quick reversal after clearing a level, distinct from a breakout that continues.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance this chart keeps getting rejected at.
screens.explanation: The ceiling price keeps failing to break is the resistance.

screens.question: A fakeout is a price move beyond a level that quickly...
screens.explanation: A quick reversal after clearing a level is what defines a fakeout.

screens.question: When is a fakeout confirmed?
options: The instant price clears the level.
Only after price reverses back following the clearing.
screens.explanation: Confirming a fakeout requires observing the reversal after the clearing.

Pausing to review whether the plan was followed, without making an immediate emotional overhaul.
Immediately doubling position size to recover the losses as fast as possible.
screens.explanation: A calm, process-focused review is commonly cited as the disciplined response, in contrast to reactive extremes.

Continue applying the plan's next genuinely valid setup calmly

Consider whether anything specific in the process needs adjusting
Continue applying the plan's next genuinely valid setup calmly

nodes.title: Lifting the Offer & Hitting the Bid

lessons.title: What Is Order Flow?
lessons.celebration: You get what order flow really means.

screens.question: What does “order flow” describe?
options: The live stream of buying, selling, and available liquidity that helps explain how price is forming.
The order in which candlesticks form across the trading day.
The sequence of chart patterns a stock cycles through.
screens.explanation: Order flow studies executed activity and available liquidity. It adds context to price, but it does not reveal every participant or guarantee the next move.

screens.question: Order flow adds context about current buying, selling, and liquidity beyond a finished price line.
screens.explanation: It can help describe current pressure, but the chart and order book are both incomplete snapshots of a changing market.

screens.question: Buyers are aggressively taking the offers on this ladder. Who is the aggressor?
screens.explanation: The side sending market orders that eat resting liquidity is the aggressor. Here that's the buyer.

screens.question: Match each term to what it really is.
pairs: The live stream of buy/sell orders
screens.explanation: Orders come first; price is the outcome; the candle is a record after the fact.

screens.question: Order flow reads the [___] between aggressive buyers and aggressive sellers.
screens.explanation: When buyers are more aggressive than sellers, price rises; when sellers dominate, it falls. It's a balance of pressure.

screens.question: Put the cause-and-effect chain in the right order.
items: Buyers and sellers place orders
Orders execute against each other
Price moves to the last fill
The candle updates on the chart
correct_order: Buyers and sellers place orders
Orders execute against each other
Price moves to the last fill
The candle updates on the chart
screens.explanation: Orders drive fills, fills set price, and only then does the chart redraw. Order-flow traders watch the front of that chain.

lessons.title: Aggressive vs. Passive Orders
lessons.celebration: You can tell takers from makers.

screens.question: What is an aggressive (market) order?
options: An order that takes whatever price is available now, removing liquidity.
An order that waits at a set price until someone trades with it.
An order that can only fill during the opening auction.
screens.explanation: A market order seeks immediate execution against available liquidity. It takes resting liquidity and can move price when nearby levels are consumed.

screens.question: What is a passive (limit) order?
options: An order resting at a chosen price, providing liquidity until someone hits it.
An order that always fills instantly at the current price.
An order the broker places automatically for you.
screens.explanation: A limit order sits in the book and waits. It can provide displayed liquidity until it is filled, changed, or canceled.

screens.question: Tap the side of the book this MARKET BUY fills against.
screens.explanation: A market buy takes the resting sell orders — it fills at the ask.

screens.question: Tap the side of the book this MARKET SELL fills against.
screens.explanation: A market sell hits the resting buy orders — it fills at the bid.

screens.question: Sort each into taker or maker.
pairs: Hitting the bid to get out fast
screens.explanation: Anything that fills immediately by crossing the spread is a taker; anything resting and waiting is a maker.

screens.question: Aggressive orders remove liquidity; passive orders provide it.
screens.explanation: Takers (market orders) consume the resting orders that makers (limit orders) supply.

screens.question: Sellers are aggressively taking the bids here. Who is the aggressor?
screens.explanation: The side sending the market orders is the aggressor — here, the seller hitting the bid.

lessons.title: The Bid, Ask & Spread
lessons.celebration: You own the bid, ask and spread.

screens.question: What is the bid?
options: The highest price buyers are currently willing to pay.
The lowest price sellers will accept.
The last price a trade printed at.
screens.explanation: The bid is the best resting buy order. Sell into it and you trade at the bid.

screens.question: What is the ask (or offer)?
options: The lowest price sellers are currently willing to accept.
The highest price buyers will pay.
The average of the day's high and low.
screens.explanation: The ask is the best resting sell order. Buy from it and you trade at the ask.

screens.question: The gap between the bid and the ask is the [___].
screens.explanation: The spread is the distance between the best buy and best sell orders — the cost of crossing from one side to the other.

screens.question: You want in NOW. Tap the side your market buy fills against.
screens.explanation: Buying immediately means paying the ask — you lift the offer.

screens.question: You want out NOW. Tap the side your market sell fills against.
screens.explanation: Selling immediately means hitting the bid.

screens.question: Match the action to the price you trade at.
screens.explanation: Buyers in a hurry pay the ask; sellers in a hurry hit the bid; the spread is the distance between them.

screens.question: A wider spread generally signals thinner liquidity.
screens.explanation: When few orders rest near price, the best bid and ask sit further apart, so the spread widens.

lessons.title: Lifting the Offer & Hitting the Bid
lessons.celebration: You can read aggression in the book.

screens.question: What does “lifting the offer” mean?
options: Aggressively buying the resting sell orders at the ask.
Cancelling your sell order above the market.
Posting a new offer higher than the last one.
screens.explanation: Lifting the offer means a buyer takes resting asks. It can move price higher when the available offers are consumed.

screens.question: Watch the offers get eaten. Someone is lifting the offer — who is the aggressor?
screens.explanation: Lifting the offer is aggressive buying: the buyer is taking the resting sell orders.

screens.question: Now the bids are getting eaten. Someone is hitting the bid — who is the aggressor?
screens.explanation: Hitting the bid is aggressive selling: the seller is taking the resting buy orders.

screens.question: When sellers keep [___] the bid, resting buy orders get eaten and price tends to fall.
screens.explanation: Hitting the bid is aggressive selling. If available bids are consumed, the next executable price can be lower.

screens.question: Match the aggression to its effect.
pairs: Only resting limit orders, no takers
screens.explanation: Aggression and available liquidity influence price, but displayed orders can also be added, canceled, or refreshed.

screens.question: A buyer wants to lift the offer. Tap the side their market order takes.
screens.explanation: Lifting the offer means taking the ask — that's where a market buy fills.

screens.question: Buyers keep lifting offers while sellers barely show. Who is in control here?
screens.explanation: Persistent lifting with little selling is aggressive demand — the buyer is the aggressor and in control.

lessons.title: What Actually Moves Price
lessons.celebration: You understand imbalance.

screens.question: What can help drive price higher over a short interval?
options: Sustained aggressive buying that consumes available offers.
The number of shares a company has outstanding.
How many candlesticks have printed that day.
screens.explanation: Sustained buying can move price through available offers. It is one input among changing quotes, cancellations, new liquidity, and broader market activity.

screens.question: A large displayed order means price will definitely hold at that level.
screens.explanation: Displayed orders can be filled, changed, canceled, or refreshed. A book snapshot is useful context, not certainty.

screens.question: A one-sided [___] of aggressive orders is what drives a strong directional move.
screens.explanation: A one-sided imbalance can contribute to a directional move, especially when it consumes nearby liquidity.

screens.question: Order these from cause to visible effect.
items: Aggressive buyers outnumber aggressive sellers
Resting offers get absorbed
Price ticks up to higher asks
A green candle prints
correct_order: Aggressive buyers outnumber aggressive sellers
Resting offers get absorbed
Price ticks up to higher asks
A green candle prints
screens.explanation: One possible sequence is imbalance → offers absorbed → higher prints → chart update. It describes a mechanism, not a prediction.

screens.question: Match the order-flow condition to what price does.
screens.explanation: These are useful tendencies, not rules. New orders, cancellations, hidden liquidity, and broader market conditions can change the read quickly.

screens.question: Price is grinding higher on relentless buying. Who is the aggressor driving it?
screens.explanation: A demand imbalance — aggressive buyers lifting offers — is pushing price up.

screens.question: To push price UP, an aggressive buyer must take which side? Tap it.
screens.explanation: Taking the ask (lifting offers) is what walks price up to higher levels.

lessons.title: Order Flow Foundations Review
lessons.celebration: Foundations mastered — you read the flow behind price.

screens.question: The offers are getting consumed. Who is the aggressor?
screens.explanation: When offers (asks) are being taken, the buyer is the aggressor — lifting the offer.

screens.question: Tap the side the MARKET BUY fills against.
screens.explanation: A market buy takes the ask.

screens.question: Tap the side the MARKET SELL fills against.
screens.explanation: A market sell hits the bid.

screens.question: Match each term to its meaning.
screens.explanation: These four ideas are the backbone of every order-flow read.

screens.question: Order flow is best described as…
options: Real-time context about buying, selling, and available liquidity.
The order in which chart patterns appear.
A schedule of company news events.
screens.explanation: It complements price action with context. It does not show every participant or guarantee an outcome.

screens.question: Rebuild the chain from order to chart.
items: Aggressive orders hit the market
They execute against resting orders
Price moves to the next level
The candle updates
correct_order: Aggressive orders hit the market
They execute against resting orders
Price moves to the next level
The candle updates
screens.explanation: Orders and fills influence the prices a chart records. Use that sequence as context, not as advance certainty about the next print.

screens.question: You buy at the ask and sell at the bid when you trade aggressively.
screens.explanation: Crossing the spread means paying the ask to buy now or hitting the bid to sell now.

screens.question: The bids are getting consumed on the ladder. Who is the aggressor?
screens.explanation: When bids are being taken, the seller is the aggressor — hitting the bid.
